articles.title: Mental Load and the Limits of Time-Based Work–Life Balance Policy
articles.authors: Iara Teixeira; Henrique Pereira
articles.abstract: Work–life balance policies can redistribute time without transferring responsibility for anticipating and coordinating care. This conceptual article asks when changes in time and task allocation permit caregivers to stop monitoring care needs. Integrating research on cognitive household labor, work–family resources, psychological recovery, and social care, it develops a model linking responsibility, authority, and the opportunity to disengage. The model proposes that continued answerability sustains monitoring and anticipatory vigilance even when another person performs the associated tasks. A dependable successor, understood as a person or institution able to assume responsibility for a defined care need, is proposed as one relational condition supporting disengagement. Gender, socioeconomic conditions, family composition, institutional recognition, and workplace arrangements shape access to this condition. The contribution is to specify how responsibility is retained or transferred within broader accounts of demands and resources, rather than to treat those accounts as exclusively concerned with time. Testable propositions distinguish changes in task performance from changes in monitoring, identify boundary conditions, and guide research across care arrangements. Using European work–life balance provisions as an illustrative policy context, the article proposes indicators for evaluating whether leave, flexibility, and services redistribute cognitive responsibility and support recovery, alongside their effects on participation in employment.

articles.title: Language-Based Mental Health Assessments Do Not Perform Evenly Across Racial and Ethnic Groups
articles.authors: Steven Mesquiti; Rebecca Carey; Nathaniel Daw; Erik C Nook
articles.abstract: Psycholinguistic tools that estimate psychological symptoms from language alone aim to provide unobtrusive assessments without needing questionnaires or clinicians. Researchers largely assume that these assessments function equivalently across demographic groups. We tested this assumption in a racially diverse sample of U.S. adults (N = 1,685; Black, Asian, Latino/Hispanic, White) who described their mental health and completed standard symptom questionnaires. Language-based markers of internalizing symptoms were often group-specific: First-person pronoun use predicted symptoms only among White participants, and sentiment varied in how strongly it tracked symptoms across groups. Machine learning models trained on White participants' language produced higher prediction error for other groups than those groups' own models did. Interpretability techniques revealed that White-trained models emphasized self-focused, agentic language more than minority groups' models. These findings indicate that linguistic tools cannot assume generalizability and must be evaluated for the populations they serve.

articles.title: Adaptation reduces perceptual effects of inter-observer metamerism with narrow-band primaries
articles.authors: Takuma Morimoto; Allie C. Schneider; Hannah Smithston
articles.abstract: Narrow-band display primaries increase observer metamerism, but to what extent does chromatic adaptation mitigate the perceptual consequences of these effects? We simulated 10,000 individualized observers viewing real-world reflectances under varied illuminants and optimized a virtual RGB display to reproduce each observer’s cone excitations. Between-observer disagreement was quantified using ΔE′ in CAM16-UCS. Without adaptation, metamerism increased as primaries narrowed, reaching a median ΔE′ of 4.8. Increasing adaptation reduced metamerism monotonically: complete adaptation reduced observers’ ΔE′ by a median of 40–67%, with the largest proportional reduction for the narrowest primaries. Adaptation to shared stimuli may therefore align visual experiences across individuals.

articles.title: Trait or Bias? Why item keying is indispensable when comparing language model responses across languages
articles.authors: Qing Li
articles.abstract: Cross-linguistic differences in large language model (LLM) questionnaire responses are increasingly interpreted as evidence of culturally patterned behaviour. Such inferences, however, assume that observed score differences reflect variation in the target construct rather than artefacts of measurement. The present study examines this assumption using three established Likert measures of social orientation administered in English and Chinese to four contemporary LLMs. Leveraging balanced-keying scales, we decompose observed cross-linguistic differences into a trait-related component and a response-bias component associated with item keying. We further test the role of item wording through keying manipulations that preserve substantive content while altering item direction. Across models and instruments, the observed language effect was found to comprise two separable components of comparable magnitude but opposite sign. The bias component was highly consistent, with English prompting producing greater agreement tendencies than Chinese prompting in every balanced-keying condition. Rewording experiments showed that the effect tracked item wording rather than substantive content, while analyses of forward-keyed instruments indicated that the two components were confounded in conventional scores. As a consequence, identical composite scores could arise from different combinations of trait-related variation and response bias. These findings do not challenge the existence of cross-linguistic variation in LLM responses. Rather, they challenge the interpretation of observed score differences as direct indicators of underlying cultural orientation. The results suggest that cross-linguistic differences in questionnaire responses reflect both construct-related variation and language-dependent response tendencies, and that balanced-keying designs are necessary to distinguish between them. More broadly, the study highlights the importance of measurement validity in cross-linguistic evaluations of LLMs and argues that prompt language should be treated as a substantive measurement variable rather than a neutral medium of expression.

articles.title: Should AI Trust Its Gut?  The Cost of Deliberative Moral Reasoning in Humans and AI
articles.authors: Simon Myers; Nick Chater
articles.abstract: People prefer deliberation to intuition, when judging how others solve hard problems, and they extend this to artificial agents. Yet in the moral domain, the preference may reverse as intuitive moral responses appear to signal good character. One explanation is that fast, intuitive responses show real emotional engagement. Since machines are thought to lack emotion, it is unclear whether a preference for intuition in the moral domain extends to AI. Across three preregistered studies (N = 2,173), we find that it does, but that it appears to be driven by commitment to moral norms and precedents rather than emotion. In Study 1, participants preferred intuitive reasoning for moral decisions and systematic reasoning for non-moral decisions, for human and AI agents alike. Intuitive moral reasoning signalled better character but was not clearly expected to produce better outcomes. In Study 2, the character preference persisted when the AI was described as being incapable of emotion. In Study 3, we held the decision fixed and varied how firmly the agent held the relevant moral norm. An agent who would never reconsider applying a moral norm was rated above one who would reconsider given sufficiently high stakes; and both above one who weighed costs and benefits case by case. Commitment raised character ratings more than expected-outcome ratings. The character-based cost of moral deliberation appears to be a cost of treating a moral norm as negotiable, and we found strong evidence that people apply this inference to machines and people alike.

articles.title: Benchmarking and Quantifying Facial Motion With Controlled Photorealistic Avatars
articles.authors: Hilal Nizamoğlu; Peer Herholz; Katharina Dobs
articles.abstract: Facial expressions are central to human social interaction, yet reliably quantifying how faces move over time remains challenging. Here, we address these limitations in three ways. First, we leverage photorealistic MetaHuman animations with precisely specified facial motion to systematically evaluate two widely used AU detection systems: AFAR and OpenFace. Four avatars were animated with identical motion parameters to generate 72 videos comprising single-AU and AU-combination sequences. Although both systems performed above chance, their performance varied substantially across AUs and avatars. Second, we introduce and validate a complementary landmark-displacement approach that directly quantifies nonrigid facial motion from tracked geometry, yielding consistent and robust motion estimates across avatars and animations. Third, we provide FACET, an open-source toolbox that integrates AU detection and landmark-based motion analysis within a unified and reproducible framework. Together, our findings reveal systematic biases in current AU-detection systems, highlight the potential of landmark-based analysis to characterize facial motion directly, and provide an open, reproducible framework for quantifying facial motion and evaluating the methods used to capture it.

articles.title: Disentangling Political Polarization in the Context of Personalized Information Environments: The Effects of Attitudinal Congruence and the Role of Individual Differences
articles.authors: Solange Vega Yanez; Cornelia Sindermann
articles.abstract: Personalized information environments have been proposed to contribute to political polarization, yet empirical findings remain mixed. The present work aimed to clarify these inconsistencies by distinguishing between different polarization outcomes and considering individual characteristics as potential moderators. In an online experiment, we tested how attitude-congruency of information environments affects issue and affective polarization regarding unconditional basic income (UBI) in Germany, and whether Intellectual Humility (IH) and Need for Cognitive Closure (NfCC) moderate these effects. N = 756 participants were exposed to one of three information environments containing predominantly attitude-congruent, attitude-incongruent, or neutral statements about UBI. Affective polarization was assessed separately as the divide in negative affective evaluations (stronger negative feelings toward the outgroup than ingroup; NAD) and the divide in positive affective evaluations (PAD; stronger positive feelings toward the ingroup than outgroup) between issue-based groups. Compared with neutral exposure, attitude-congruent information increased issue polarization, NAD, and PAD. Attitude-incongruent information decreased issue polarization but  had no signficant effect on either affective divide. IH was positively associated with and moderated effects on PAD. NfCC showed no effects. Findings highlight the importance of distinguishing between polarization outcomes and suggest that positive and negative affective intergroup divides may show different associations with individual characteristics.

articles.title: Artificial Agents as Leaders and Followers: An Integrative Role-Congruity Review
articles.authors: Christoph Daldrop; Annabelle Ludwig; Claudia Buengeler
articles.abstract: Artificial agents such as algorithms, virtual agents, and robots increasingly occupy organizational roles as leaders, followers, and partners. However, evidence on how people evaluate these nonhuman role occupants is mixed. We systematically review 107 empirical studies across management, psychology, engineering, and computer science through a role-congruity lens. A consistent pattern emerges: Artificial agents in leader roles face role incongruity, driven largely by perceived deficits in morality (e.g., fairness, trustworthiness). Agents in follower roles are evaluated as largely congruent with role expectations. Agents in partner and teammate roles show conditional congruity that depends on task context and design-based social cues (e.g., appearance, voice). We integrate these patterns into the Artificial Agent Role Congruity (AARC) model, a conceptual model that extends role congruity theory to artificial agents: perceived role (in)congruity occurs when observers compare role prescriptions with the attributes they ascribe to an agent from its design-based cues along a task dimension (competence, assertiveness) and a social-emotional dimension (warmth, morality). Based on this synthesis, we outline theoretical extensions, an agenda for future research, and guidance for managers and designers deploying artificial agents in organizational roles.

articles.title: A Practical Guide to Cross-Cultural Research with eHRAF
articles.authors: Zachary H Garfield; Rohan Kapitány; Sheina Lew-Levy
articles.abstract: The electronic Human Relations Area Files (eHRAF) World Cultures database indexes primary ethnographic documents at the paragraph level, allowing researchers to assemble systematic samples of text on a wide range of topics and across diverse societies. Unlike some other cross-cultural databases, eHRAF does not provide precoded society-level variables. It provides source text from which researchers can construct variables, and as such offers researchers greater flexibility in their ability to operationalize variables. We present an eight-step workflow for building a coded cross-cultural dataset from eHRAF: 1) formulating a question suited to the ethnographic record; 2) selecting Outline of Cultural Materials codes and constructing a search; 3) defining the unit of analysis and data structure; 4) addressing research ethics and working within the terms of service; 5) assembling a database; 6) developing and piloting a coding scheme; 7) training coders and assessing reliability; and 8) analyzing nested data. Drawing on our published research and experience supervising student projects, we identify common challenges, offer practical guidelines, and provide a reporting checklist. The workflow is intended to make eHRAF-based research more accessible and prevalent within the fields of behavioral and cultural research, while facilitating a more systematic, transparent, and reproducible approach.

articles.title: Inconclusive mediated effect of empathy on perceived stress among nurses: A comment on Wang et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles.abstract: Using the covariance matrix reported by Wang et al., we reexamined the evidence underlying their proposed mediation model relating empathy to lower perceived stress. We show that the same pattern of associations can be accounted for by an alternative latent-variable model that does not assume the causal sequence proposed by the original authors. In this alternative formulation, self-reported empathy, occupational commitment, ego-resilience, and perceived stress are treated as indicators of a broader latent trait, core self-evaluation. The findings illustrate a general challenge in psychological research: a single covariance structure may be consistent with multiple theoretically plausible explanations. As a result, correlational data alone rarely provide a sufficient basis for favoring one theoretical account over another. We therefore argue that the evaluation of competing models should become a routine component of efforts to draw conclusions about psychological processes from observational data.

articles.title: Addressing Heterogeneity with Bayesian Meta-Analytic Mixture Modelling
articles.authors: Maximilian Maier
articles.abstract: Unexplained heterogeneity is a pervasive challenge that undermines the validity of meta-analytic inferences, often even after accounting for plausible moderators. To address this issue, this paper introduces a Bayesian meta-analytic mixture modelling approach that enables data-driven clustering of effect sizes. The resulting mixture components can subsequently be interpreted in light of study characteristics and domain knowledge, providing a principled, data-driven way to model and explore heterogeneity. To accommodate publication bias, I combine the mixture modelling framework with selection models. The number of mixture components and the presence and type of publication bias can be evaluated using Bayes factors. Three simulation studies validate the method and compare it to existing publication bias correction methods. Results show that wrongly assuming effect sizes follow a single normal distribution can substantially distort inferences from standard publication bias correction methods, which can be addressed by using meta-analytic mixture modelling. Finally, I illustrate the new method on a recent high-profilemeta-analysis on nudging. To facilitate application in practice, I implemented the methods in the R-package metamix.

articles.title: The Deepfake Discount: Believing Erotic Images Are AI-Generated Reduces Affective Responses
articles.authors: Ana Neves; Marco VIOLA; Marco Sperduti; Guido Corradi; Antonio Olivera-LaRosa; Alessandro Ansani; Marco Marini; Dominique Makowski
articles.abstract: The proliferation of AI-generated content raises the question of whether beliefs about a stimulus’s origin alter emotional responses to it. Across two studies, we conceptually replicated and extended Marini et al. (2024) by presenting heterosexual participants (Study 1: N = 705; Study 2: N = 261) with erotic (Studies 1 and 2) and non-erotic (Study 1) images from validated databases (NAPS and NAPS ERO). Unbeknownst to participants, all stimuli were real photographs, each randomly labelled as “Photograph” or “AI-generated”. Participants rated sexual arousal, enticement, and valence for each image, and later judged their agreement with the labels. Images labelled as AI-generated received lower affective ratings, but this effect was small and driven primarily by male participants. Gender differences were robust yet context dependent: males yielded more robust differences, partially driven by a higher baseline arousal response. However, image of couples (Study 2), that females rated as more arousing, narrowed the gender gap found in Study 1. Critically, the effect of the labels interacted with participant’s own beliefs: photograph-labelled images were rated more arousing than AI-labelled only when participants’ subsequent belief ratings were congruent with the label, and the difference between labels reversed when opposite beliefs were reported, suggesting a complex relationship between emotion and reality beliefs. Individual-level differences in AI attitudes, pornography consumption, and sexual activity showed no reliable modulation of the labels effect. These findings suggest that the anti-AI bias is best understood as a belief-sensitive authenticity effect rather than a uniform response to AI labels, with implications for research using synthetic stimuli and for policies mandating disclosure of AI-generated content.

articles.title: Induction and Overreach in the Science of Consciousness
articles.authors: Matthew Phillip Gunn; Christine C. Minton; Chienyem A. Nweke
articles.abstract: Induction shapes consciousness science as researchers infer experience, generalizing neural signatures, and project across contexts. While deduction sets ideals of certainty, induction guides experimentation and decision-making. This article provides a synoptic analysis of induction’s role in consciousness science by surveying its philosophical background, from Aristotle and Hume to Popper, Salmon, and Peirce, and its formalization in Bayesian and predictive-processing frameworks. This manuscript then examines how induction operates across neuroimaging, comparative cognition, and clinical contexts, highlighting successes (pattern detection, anesthesia monitoring, covert awareness detection) and structural risks (correlation–causation slippage, overgeneralization, anthropomorphism, and high-stakes misclassification). Recent sufficiency-oriented syntheses (e.g., Coppola, 2025; Mashour et al., 2020; Hohwy et al., 2020) exemplify both the power and the perils of inductive generalization, extending correlational findings into claims of ontological sufficiency. Building on recent critiques and adversarial comparisons of leading theories, this article argues for an explicitly deflationary program that keeps induction indispensable but bounded. The core tools are: (i) operational vocabularies distinguishing constructs (access, arousal, valuation, metacognition); (ii) transparent bridge principles linking observables to experiences; and (iii) prediction tables that register both positive predictions and falsifiers. This pragmatic framework does not solve Hume’s problem; it makes our inductive commitments tractable, testable, and ethically responsible. Consciousness science should remain inductive, just not inflationary. To demonstrate this framework’s tractability, the paper introduces examples of bridge principles and quantitative criteria for “bounded” inference, including Bayesian priors, model-comparison metrics, and causal graphs. Ethical and institutional dimensions are expanded to include AI, animal, and algorithmic induction. These additions link philosophical modesty with methodological implementation and moral accountability.

articles.title: Measuring heart and breath: BRAMS-Bio-Box (B3), a wearable  open-source physiology recording platform
articles.authors: Mehrdad Bahadori; Jérémie Voix; Simone Dalla Bella; Floris Tijmen van Vugt
articles.abstract: Psychology and social neuroscience study the biological basis of real-world interactive behaviors, such as dancing or playing music in groups. Autonomic nervous system reactivity, assessed through cardiac and respiratory signals, plays an important role in these behaviors. However, affordable, scientifically validated, research-grade devices for synchronous, real-time physiological monitoring of multiple individuals in natural settings remain scarce. We propose a wearable open-source physiological monitoring device, the BRAMS-Bio-Box (B3), that can record cardiac and respiratory signals simultaneously from multiple individuals. B3 can be built cost-effectively using open-source blueprints and software we provide to yield a transparent, flexible option for research-grade physiological data collection. We empirically validated B3 against a widely used reference device in nine participants performing various motor and guided-respiration tasks. Heart rate (HR) and heart rate variability (HRV) were derived from electrocardiographic (ECG) signals, while respiratory sensors were evaluated for respiration rate and the accuracy and consistency of exhalation event detection. B3 derived HR and HRV closely matched reference measures across tasks, with high quality ECG recordings and minimal data loss, except during vigorous arm swinging. Respiratory rate and pattern metrics, including exhalation peak timing, also showed strong agreement. The B3 thermistor accurately tracked respiration rate even at higher breathing frequencies, although minor timing offsets occurred during some guided respiration segments. Overall, B3 performed comparably to the reference system for cardiac and respiratory measures, offering an affordable, open-source solution for physiological monitoring in real-world interactive settings.

articles.title: The Effects of Target Characteristics on Public Support for Hate Speech Laws
articles.authors: Jesper Rasmussen
articles.abstract: Does the target of speech shape public support for hate speech laws? Regulating hate speech is controversial, partly because partisans are assumed to disagree over which groups such laws should protect. This article conducts a comprehensive test of how support for hate speech laws varies across partisan lines when speech targets ethnic, religious, gender, or political groups. Based on conjoint experiments in Denmark and the United States, the results show that support for regulation increases by up to 32 percentage points when severity increases from “incivility” to “incitement to violence.” Target characteristics increase support for regulation by up to 6.3 percentage points and exert the strongest effects when speech targets ethnic and religious groups rather than gender or political groups. These effects persist when severity is held constant and are broadly stable across severity levels. They are also heterogeneous across partisan groups, mostly ranging from 3 to 7.2 percentage points, with one exception reaching 11.9 percentage points. In neither country are partisans more willing to regulate hate speech targeting their political opponents than hate speech targeting their political allies. Overall, severity has the strongest effect on support for hate speech regulation, while target characteristics have smaller, heterogeneous effects that are largest when speech targets ethnic or religious groups.

articles.title: Does Calling an AI Advisor "Agentic" Make People Trust It More? An Online Experiment on Trust and Financial Risk-Taking
articles.authors: Michele Lodetti
articles.abstract: AI financial advisors are increasingly presented as autonomous agents that reason and act on their own. Theory suggests that such agency cues should raise perceptions of an AI's ability and integrity, but not its benevolence, and that trust in its ability and integrity should increase willingness to take financial risks. I tested these predictions in a between-subjects experiment with 195 UK adults, with the hypotheses specified before data collection. Participants met an AI advisor framed either as a rule-based system or as an autonomous advisor, received the same final advice and allocated a hypothetical £1,000 between a low-risk and a high-risk investment. The framing increased perceived agency (Hedges' g = 0.46) but did not detectably change trust in the advisor's ability (g = 0.18, 95% CI [−0.11, 0.46]), integrity (g = −0.10) or benevolence (g = 0.00). Bayes factors favoured the null hypothesis for all three dimensions (BF01 = 3.2 to 6.4), and equivalence tests ruled out medium-sized effects on integrity and benevolence, though not on ability. Neither trust in ability nor trust in integrity was significantly related to risk-taking, and there was no evidence of mediation. Yet perceived agency correlated with every trust dimension (r = .35 to .50). Describing the advisor as agentic changed what people thought the system was but did not detectably change whether they trusted it. For human-machine communication research, the findings caution against reading correlations between perceived machine agency and trust as causal, and suggest that agency framing is a weak lever for trust in high-stakes advice.

articles.title: Mapping adolescent social media use: A scoping review
articles.authors: Jade Davies; Louise Black; Jo Hickman Dunne; Margarita Panayiotou
articles.abstract: Research on the impact of social media use on adolescent mental health lacks consensus, likely exacerbated by the field’s reliance on coarse measures like time spent online. More granular conceptualisations of use have been proposed as a way to clarify when, why, and for whom social media use may be beneficial, neutral, or harmful. In this scoping review, we used the Multidimensional Model of Social Media Use (Yang et al., 2021) as a framework to systematically map the diversity of adolescent social media use. Specifically, we examined how adolescents describe their social media use, how researchers quantify this use and the degree of (dis)alignment between the two. In total, we reviewed 6,822 articles for inclusion, with 522 meeting the inclusion criteria. Adolescents’ qualitative accounts portrayed social media use as complex, fluid, and multi dimensional, involving a wide range of activities, motivational functions, and communication partners. We draw on these accounts to extend the Multidimensional Model, specifying more precise categories of activity, motivation, and communication partner, and incorporating additional contextual dimensions that characterise adolescents’ social media use. Mapping quantitative studies onto this framework revealed broad conceptual overlap but substantial methodological fragmentation, including heterogeneous and often unvalidated measures. The extended framework developed through this review provides a more precise foundation for future empirical work examining links between social media use and mental health and highlights the need for research designs capable of capturing the dynamic nature of adolescent social media use. Assessing adolescents’ views on the framework represents an important next step.

articles.title: Reconsidering Global Comparisons of Scientist Trustworthiness
articles.authors: Yuke Yang; Zhihao Ma
articles.abstract: In a reanalysis of perceived scientist trustworthiness across 68 countries/regions, measurement-aligned indicated limitations in the cross-national comparability of the original measurement structure. Some country/region rankings and predictor associations varied across alternative scoring approaches, suggesting the value of considering measurement invariance when interpreting cross-national findings. Future research could use diverse methods to strengthen cross-cultural measurement validity.

articles.title: Interactional Fingerprints of Personality: Big Five Traits Predict Conversational Behavior Similarly Across Face-to-Face and Video-Mediated Initial Interactions
articles.authors: Ville Johannes Harjunen; Leevi Lintunen; Sami Hyttinen; Patrick Ghaemmaghami; Santeri Lepistö; Markus Söderman; Pyry Heikkinen; Anssi Peräkylä; Niklas Ravaja; Jan Lindström
articles.abstract: Little is known about how Big Five personality traits manifest in specific conversational behaviors or whether these associations depend on the communication medium. We examined 154 individuals interacting with strangers face-to-face or via video. Using manual annotations, computer vision, and LLMs, we examined actor and partner personality associations with turn-taking dynamics, engagement signalling, and topic development. Higher actor and partner extraversion predicted faster turn-taking and pronounced engagement signalling, whereas actor openness predicted slower turn-taking and reduced engagement signalling. In actors, conscientiousness predicted nodding and in partners it predicted broader topic exploration. However, we found no evidence that these associations differed between face-to-face and video-mediated interaction. Personality thus shapes conversational behavior and these interactional fingerprints appear to survive technological transmission.

articles.title: AI-Podcast Misinformation: Testing Active versus Passive Inoculations
articles.authors: Paul McIlhiney; Emily Rebecca Spearing; Ullrich K. H. Ecker
articles.abstract: Realistic, misleading AI-generated audio content is a new threat to digital-media consumers. This study examined the effects of misleading AI-generated podcasts that presented false claims about nanoparticles in sunscreen (Experiment 1; N = 463), or microwaves damaging foods (Experiment 2; N = 500). U.S. participants either received a misleading podcast, misleading article, or a neutral podcast (control). To test interventions, misleading podcasts were preceded by either a passive inoculation explaining how AI-generated information can deceive, an active inoculation that added an educational activity, or no intervention. The podcast and article produced comparable increases in misinformed beliefs. Both inoculations significantly reduced general trust in AI-generated information and attenuated the podcast’s impact on beliefs. Results demonstrate that AI-generated audio can influence health-related beliefs as strongly as text-based misinformation, and that brief AI-source-focused inoculations can mitigate, but not eliminate, its persuasive impact. Findings inform interventions targeting emerging forms of AI-driven misinformation.

articles.title: Right Error Wrong Time: Condition-Dependent Fast and Slow Errors Distort Architecture Inference in Systems Factorial Technology
articles.authors: Hang Qian; Paul Michael Garrett; Philip L. Smith; Daniel R. Little
articles.abstract: Systems Factorial Technology infers processing architecture from response-time distributions obtained under factorial manipulations of information quality. These analysis are conventionally restricted to correct responses, leaving unclear whether condition-dependent errors can distort the architecture-diagnostic survivor interaction contrast (SIC). We used diffusion-model simulations to examine whether SIC-based diagnoses remain valid when errors differ in prevalence and timing across the high–high, high–low, low–high, and low–low conditions. We first implemented coactive processing using the partitioned circular diffusion model under AND and OR task rules. Cross-trial variability in drift magnitude produced slow errors, whereas variability in the decision boundary produced fast errors. Although the expected stochastic ordering of the correct-response survivor functions was generally preserved, both mechanisms progressively attenuated the characteristic negative-then-positive coactive SIC, causing it to resemble the entirely positive signature of parallel self-terminating processing. We then generalized the analysis to a parallel self-terminating architecture implemented using linear-drift, linear-infinitesimal-variance model. Racing generated slow errors even without cross-trial drift-rate variability, but the expected positive SIC remained robust while the error pattern was relatively similar across factorial conditions. Adding drift-rate variability differentiated the condition-specific error patterns and progressively weakened the SIC. These findings show that presence of errors compromises architectural diagnosis when their timing and prevalence differ across four factorial conditions, causing correct-response selection to reshape the contributing RT distributions unequally. Conditional accuracy functions provide a practical companion measure for identifying this risk.

articles.title: Therapeutic Listening for Stress Reduction in Adolescents: A Mixed-Methods Pilot Study Comparing Binaural Beats and Singing Bowl Sound
articles.authors: Xuanyi Sophia Wang; Jiayue Cecilia Wu
articles.abstract: Adolescents with chronic academic stress may benefit from accessible, non-pharmacological approaches to stress management. In this mixed-methods pilot study, six Grade 11 students completed a randomized, counterbalanced within-subject crossover design to compare the immediate effects of binaural-beat and singing-bowl listening. Each condition was preceded by a 3-min baseline and followed by physiological, device-derived, subjective, and qualitative assessments. Outcomes were heart rate, heart-rate variability (RMSSD), NeuroSky-derived Attention and Meditation indices, self-reported positive affect, negative affect, calmness, and open-ended reflections. Physiological responses varied widely across participants and no clear condition-level advantage was observed for heart rate, RMSSD or affective ratings. Five of six participants showed an increased NeuroSky-derived Meditation-index change in response to singing-bowl listening. All six participants selected the singing-bowl condition as more effective in promoting relaxation. In the qualitative reflections, people more often described the listening to singing bowls as calming, immersive and compatible with breathing. The results are exploratory and do not demonstrate therapeutic superiority or neural entrainment. They propose that perceptual comfort, attentional engagement and individual listening experience may be important components of sound-based stress regulation in adolescents.

articles.title: The ‘Social Matrix’: Developing and testing a common framework for measuring perceptions of social constructs across groups and institutions
articles.authors: Michelle Degli Esposti; Eduardo Viegas da Silva; Rafaela Costa Martins; Gessyka Wanglon Veleda; Juliana Costa da Silva; Cauane Blumenberg; Joseph Murray
articles.abstract: How individuals perceive their social worlds is fundamental to the study of human behaviour, health, and wellbeing. However, component constructs such as perceived trust, legitimacy, and social cohesion have been typically studied in isolation or in relation to specific social groups and institutions, limiting our understanding of how these perceptions are interconnected. Here, we present the Social Matrix, a common framework and measurement instrument designed to efficiently measure multiple social perceptions concurrently across different social groups and institutions. Following systematic development, expert review and cultural adaptation, we piloted the instrument among 784 participants using a cross-sectional online survey among three developmentally distinct age groups (child (11-14 years), n=197; adolescence (15-18 years), n=210; adults (19-59 years), n=377) in Brazil. We found encouraging evidence of convergent validity with established measures and limited item redundancy. Latent profile analyses identified four distinct patterns of social perceptions across age groups, including generalised positive and negative profiles and contrasting perceptions of civic versus security institutions. Generalised negative perceptions were associated with lower socioeconomic position and fewer years of education among adults. These findings suggest that perceptions of social groups and institutions are interconnected but differentiated, with meaningful differential patterns between individuals. The Social Matrix provides a foundation for investigating how individuals represent their wider social worlds and a platform for investigating how these representations may link societal conditions to individual behaviour and collective outcomes, thereby supporting theoretical and empirical research bridging the macro-micro gap.

articles.title: From Psychological States to Survey Responses: A Theory of Latent States and Response Styles
articles.authors: Jess Grimmond; Scott Brown; Quentin Frederik Gronau; Guy Hawkins
articles.abstract:
Research on individual differences relies heavily on self-report measures, yet observed
responses often reflect both the psychological attributes being assessed and the response
processes individuals use when communicating those attributes. We propose a theory of
self-report responding in which survey constructs and response styles represent distinct sources of
individual differences that jointly determine observed responses. We formalise this account in the
Latent State and Response Style (LASARS) model, an ordinal-probit framework that separates
these sources of variance, yielding cleaner estimates of survey constructs while simultaneously
producing interpretable measures of response behaviour. LASARS conceptualises response styles
as stable, multidimensional individual differences in how respondents translate internal
experiences into response options. This framework generates novel predictions regarding the
structure, stability, and generalisability of response styles. Across a series of empirical studies, we
show that response styles can be selectively modified by task demands without corresponding
changes in substantive scores, and that they exhibit substantial stability across time and
measurement instruments, often matching or exceeding the stability of the psychological
constructs they accompany. We further demonstrate that response style information obtained from
one measure can be used to separate stylistic and substantive variance in a different measure, even
when that measure alone cannot identify the two sources of variation. Together, these findings
support a view of response styles as meaningful individual differences rather than mere
measurement error and provide a framework for improving the measurement and interpretation of
individual differences across psychological research.

articles_hidden.title: To replicate or not to replicate? My nine failures to publish a successful replication
articles_hidden.authors: Sharon Gilaie-Dotan
articles_hidden.abstract: Simmons, Nelson, and Simonsohn (2011) proposed disclosure-based practices — a priori power analyses, full reporting of conditions and exclusions, results reported with and without exclusions applied — as a remedy for the replication crisis. Following these practices explicitly, our lab attempted to publish an online replication and extension of our earlier PNAS findings on image size and memory, expecting that doing so would make publication straightforward. It did not. Nine submissions over 2.5 years were unsuccessful (eight rejections and one withdrawal), largely on the grounds that a transparent, successful replication lacked sufficient theoretical novelty to warrant publication on its own; it was accepted only after this framing was substantially minimized in favor of additional analyses and an alternative theoretical framework. Here, I reflect on this experience, raise open questions about whether the field's evaluation of replications has kept pace with its stated commitment to them, and offer recommendations for future practices.

articles_hidden.title: Developmental changes in children’s production of line drawings in global contexts: Evidence from Kisumu, Kenya
articles_hidden.authors: Rebecca Zhu; Joab Ochieng Arieda; Tabitha Nduku; Zachary Watson; Tarun Sepuri; Bria Long; Judith Fan; Michael C. Frank
articles_hidden.abstract: Children growing up in environments with many drawing opportunities improve dramatically at producing recognizable drawings over the course of childhood. Does this same developmental trajectory hold for children growing up in environments with fewer drawing opportunities? We measured children’s ability to produce recognizable drawings in a context where children have relatively fewer drawing opportunities and experiences with visual media, specifically Kisumu, Kenya. By leveraging within-context variation in children’s drawing experience, we estimated the strength of the association between how often a child draws and how recognizable their drawings are. A preregistered sample of 120 4- to 9-year-olds drew 12 object categories in random order. Children produced more recognizable drawings with age, even after controlling for their tracing abilities. Moreover, younger children with more drawing experience produced more recognizable drawings, even after controlling for tracing ability and other home environment variables. These results suggest commonalities in drawing development across cultures and document the experience-dependence of drawing development in global contexts.

articles_hidden.title: The Role of Parental Reflective Functioning in the Association Between Parental and Youth Emotion Regulation Among Youth With Serious Mental Health Challenges
articles_hidden.authors: Laura Daari; Sebastian Dys; Marlene Moretti
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Parental and adolescent emotion regulation are associated, yet the role of parental reflective functioning (PRF) as a relational pathway linking them remains largely unexamined, particularly among parents of youth with serious mental health challenges.

Methods: Parents (N = 372) of adolescents (ages 9–19) with serious mental health challenges reported on their own emotion regulation within the parent–adolescent relationship, PRF, and their adolescent's emotion regulation. Structural equation modelling with bootstrapped indirect effects examined direct and indirect associations between parental emotion regulation (dysregulation, suppression), PRF facets (prementalizing, certainty about mental states, and interest and curiosity in mental states), and adolescent emotion regulation (dysregulation, suppression). 

Results: Parental dysregulation was positively associated with adolescent dysregulation and suppression, whereas parental suppression showed no direct associations with adolescent outcomes. All three PRF facets were associated with adolescent emotion regulation: greater prementalizing with greater youth dysregulation; greater certainty with lower youth dysregulation and suppression; and greater interest and curiosity unexpectedly with greater youth dysregulation and suppression. Three indirect associations emerged: parental dysregulation was associated with adolescent dysregulation through higher prementalizing and, separately, through lower certainty about mental states, and parental suppression was associated with lower adolescent suppression through lower interest and curiosity.

Conclusions:  Parental dysregulation was associated with adolescent emotion regulation in this clinical sample, relating to adolescent dysregulation through both prementalizing and certainty. Less consistent with prior research, interest and curiosity was associated with poorer adolescent emotion regulation, raising the possibility that this facet relates differently in clinical, adolescent populations than in the community samples of younger children where it has typically been studied. These findings suggest PRF facets may represent differentiated intervention targets, and highlight the need for longitudinal, multi-informant research to establish temporal ordering.

Keywords: emotion regulation; parental reflective functioning; mentalizing; parenting; adolescents; parent–child relationship

articles_hidden.title: Interoceptive Processing in Boredom Proneness: Sensing Without Making Sense
articles_hidden.authors: Chantal Trudel; James Danckert
articles_hidden.abstract:
Boredom proneness has been linked to a disrupted relationship with one's internal states, yet the
mechanism underlying this disruption remains unclear. One possibility is that this disruption
reflects a difficulty in translating interoceptive signals into meaningful predictions about internal
states, rather than a basic failure to detect them. Across two studies, we examined whether this
disrupted relationship reflects interpretive challenges, a deficit in cardiac interoceptive accuracy,
or both. Study 1 (N = 124) was a direct replication confirming that highly boredom prone
individuals report attending intensely to bodily sensations while struggling to interpret them — a
pattern that held across a combined sample of 350 adults and yielded moderate-to-strong
correlations with established measures of self-focused attention and interoceptive sensory
confusion. Study 2 (N = 121) administered a heartbeat counting task to determine whether this
disrupted relationship was due to deficient interoceptive processing or interpretive failure.
Boredom proneness was unrelated to objective heartbeat counting accuracy but remained
associated with self-reported interoceptive sensory confusion. Converging with Study 1, this
pattern suggests that boredom proneness is best characterized by a difficulty in interpreting internal
signals than by a basic interoceptive perceptual deficit. Together, these findings are consistent with
predictive processing accounts of boredom proneness where those high in trait boredom struggle
to generate meaningful predictions from interoceptive cues. Whether this dissociation between
self-reported and objective cardiac interoception generalizes across different measurement
approaches and populations remains an open question that future work could examine using more
sensitive interoceptive tasks and trial-level prediction error metrics.

articles_hidden.title: Incentivizing Open Science: Examining the Open Data Citation Advantage in Visual Search Research
articles_hidden.authors: Jonathan Nir
articles_hidden.abstract:
In the wake of psychology’s credibility revolution, open science practices such as data sharing have become more prevalent, yet researchers often cite a lack of professional incentives as a barrier to adoption. This report examines the association between data sharing and scholarly impact in visual search and eye-movement literature, building on the systematic audit by Godwin et al. (2025).
I extended their dataset with bibliometric metadata from the OpenAlex registry and compared field-normalized, accumulated, and time-resolved citation impact between articles that did and did not share data. Although articles that shared data showed a small citation advantage in unadjusted analyses, this difference was no longer statistically significant after adjusting for publication characteristics such as publication age and journal citedness. A time-resolved analysis revealed a small association between sharing status and the trajectory of citation accrual, but did not establish a robust early citation advantage. Citation impact also did not differ by data granularity: sharing fine-grained fixation-level data did not confer greater benefit than sharing coarser participant-level summaries.
These observational findings provide no robust evidence of an overall citation advantage associated with data sharing in this research domain, nor of an additional advantage for finer-grained data.  They do not establish that data sharing has no citation benefit, but highlight the importance of examining how its association with scholarly impact varies across research contexts and over time.

articles_hidden.title: More Visibility for Diversity? A Systematic Review of LGBTQ+ Representation in Educational Psychology Journals
articles_hidden.authors: Valentin Emslander; Oliver Adam Kluge; Christoph Niepel
articles_hidden.abstract: Students identifying as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, or otherwise non-heterosexual or non-cisgender (LGBTQ+) are increasingly represented. However, they still face additional challenges in educational settings, so Educational Psychology needs to research these issues. In this preregistered systematic scientometric literature review, we investigate (a) the extent of LGBTQ+ centered research in Educational Psychology journals, (b) common themes and trends, and discuss systematic gaps for future research. After searching all 41,992 articles on ERIC, published in the most impactful (Q1 and Q2) Educational Psychology journals, we combined scientometric-quantitative and qualitative methods to review 68 eligible articles. We found a surge in publications from 2000 onward, driven by special issues. For almost half of these high-impact journals, we found no published articles on LGBTQ+ issues on ERIC; most publish only a few per thousand, even though this topic falls within their scope. Most often, these articles were empirical, correlational, and US-based, with inconsistent measures of LGBTQ+ identities. Through qualitative thematic analysis, we identified seven research themes and highlighted pertinent research gaps. To strengthen the evidence base in the field, future research should conduct rigorous longitudinal and intervention studies with culturally diverse samples and adhere to open science standards.

articles_hidden.title: Cross-Modal Associations in Creativity: Evaluating Word-Image Pairing in Humans and Large Language Models
articles_hidden.authors: Eva Illion; Linxuan Wang; Liane Gabora
articles_hidden.abstract: Given differences in the associative memory architectures of humans and AI, it is not clear whether AI generates and interprets visual-linguistic associations the way humans do. To investigate this, human participants and two large language models (LLMs), ChatGPT and Gemini, were asked to generate novel words and corresponding images that form meaningfully linked dyads. The LLMs and a second group of human participants were presented with shuffled sets of these words and images and asked to rematch them in ways they felt were most meaningful. Humans performed similarly regardless of whether the pairs were human or LLM-generated, while LLMs were better at matching LLM-generated pairs. Overall, LLMs outperformed humans at recovering the intended pairings. These findings suggest that despite architectural differences, the way in which AI generates and detects associations between language and visual stimuli is not only like that of humans, but they may be superior at recognizing cross-domain associations that humans find meaningful.

articles_hidden.title: Testing causal mechanisms of transdiagnostic dissociation in 16-to-25-year-olds: A randomised multiple baseline experimental design series using brief targeted CBT.
articles_hidden.authors: Emma Černis; Milan Antonovic; Gwynnevere Suter
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
Dissociative experiences are common and transdiagnostic. Yet causal evidence for psychological mechanisms of dissociation remains scarce, particularly in youth. Our group has developed a translational cognitive-behavioural model of a subset of common dissociative experiences (FSA-dissociation), but causal relationships proposed within this model remain to be tested.

Aims
This study sought to experimentally test three causal relationships proposed in the FSA-dissociation CBT model using an interventionist-causal paradigm. A benefit of this method is the opportunity it provides to simultaneously develop targeted therapeutic techniques whilst empirically testing the underlying theory.
Method
We conducted a randomised multiple baseline experimental design study with nine NHS patients (aged 16 to 23), targeting three hypothesised mechanisms of change: cognitive appraisals of dissociation, perseverative thinking, and affect intolerance. The study was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06054009). Each participant received four sessions of individual CBT with a clinical psychologist targeting one hypothesised mechanism. 

Results
Analysis indicated successful targeting of cognitive appraisals, and partial success for affect intolerance and perseverative thinking. Findings tentatively support cognitive appraisals and affect intolerance as candidate causal mechanisms in youth dissociation. Any effect of targeting perseverative thinking was better accounted for by reduced cognitive appraisals. 

Discussion
Although phase instability limited inference, this study offers novel causal insights into transdiagnostic dissociation and informs early-stage treatment development for this presentation. Namely, it suggests that future psychological interventions for transdiagnostic dissociation in youth should incorporate targeting of cognitive appraisals, but that further research is required to determine whether affect intolerance constitutes a therapeutic target in this context.

articles_hidden.title: Attachment and Caregiving as Social Allostatic Inference: An Updated Social Neuroscience Account from Single Brains to Dyads
articles_hidden.authors: Pascal Vrticka; Tsachi Ein-Dor
articles_hidden.abstract: Humans are highly social, and much of that sociality is regulatory: individuals manage the demands placed upon their bodies not only alone but through and with others. Attachment science has pursued how the brain accomplishes this for the better part of a century, and its most recent contribution has been neurobiological. Within the Social Neuroscience of Human Attachment (SoNeAt) programme, we previously specified a neuroanatomical architecture of two interacting systems and four domain-general modules for organised attachment, extended it to attachment disruption and disorganisation, and moved it from single brains to dyads through hyperscanning as part of Relational Neuroscience. What that work established energetically, through social allostasis, it did not specify computationally. Here we close that gap. Drawing on active inference, allostasis as interoceptive inference, and recent constructs of attachment as prediction, we propose the term social allostatic inference: the attachment system is one predictive-allostatic loop, the four modules are its successive stages, and organised, disrupted, and disorganised attachment are characteristic settings of the precision parameters that govern it. We extend the account to the caregiving system, which shares this architecture but infers rather than senses both the error that initiates its loop and the signal that terminates it. At the level of the dyad, interpersonal neural and bio-behavioural synchrony are read as indices of where regulatory work is invested rather than of bond quality directly. We address persistent misconceptions in trauma-informed practice and set out a measurement programme.

articles_hidden.title: Day by Day, Bit by Bit: Knowledge Building Mechanisms Evolve with Development
articles_hidden.authors: Layla Unger; Olivera Savic; Vladimir Sloutsky
articles_hidden.abstract: Much of human knowledge distills patterns that are consistent across many similar experiences over time, such as the typical layout of a bedroom. This is particularly true of word knowledge. The thousands of words we learn form a stable, interconnected network of word meanings that capture regularities in the way words are typically combined to express ideas, such as that “oranges” are something you can “eat” and similar to “apples”. Yet, we know surprisingly little about accumulating knowledge from regularities over time, especially in childhood when building knowledge is paramount. Here, we investigated 4-6-year-old children’s abilities to accumulate interconnected word knowledge from regularities experienced repeatedly over a month. Younger children appeared to relearn the regularities anew at each exposure, whereas older children accumulated increasingly strong connections across encounters. These findings point to substantial developmental changes in gradual learning processes that build knowledge over time.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond conflict adaptation: Affectively experiencing and observing conflict enhance performance across conflict and non-conflict trials
articles_hidden.authors: YueChang Wang; Shuangqing Si; Gilles Pourtois; Qian Yang
articles_hidden.abstract: Conflict processing typically elicits control adjustments, as expressed by the Conflict Adaptation Effect (CAE), which could be mediated by negative affect. Recent findings further suggest that the affective experience of conflict, even without responding, improves subsequent performance on both conflict and non-conflict trials, suggesting a broader enhancement of cognitive control. To clarify the mechanisms underlying this general benefit resulting from the affective experience of conflict, the present study conducted three behavioral experiments using a confound-minimized Stroop task. Experiment 1 compared a standard “Do-do” condition with an “Experience-do” condition, where participants experienced conflict at the affective level in a non-response phase first, before carrying out the Stroop task during a second one. Experiment 2 replaced “Experience-do” with a “Look-do” condition, where participants merely observed the Stroop stimulus first (without the need to experience it at the affective level), before completing the Stroop task. Experiment 3 introduced a “Judgement-do” condition, directing attention to a conflict-unrelated feature. We found that conflict elicited negative affect and a reliable CAE in all “Do-do” conditions. Crucially, both affective experience (Experiment 1) and mere observation (Experiment 2) of conflict produced general performance improvements extending from incongruent to congruent trials (i.e., a General Adaptation Effect – GAE), with a larger benefit in Experiment 1 than 2. This improvement disappeared when attention was directed to a conflict-unrelated feature (Experiment 3), suggesting that it is tied to conflict-related processing. These findings suggest that affectively experiencing or simply observing conflict is sufficient to enhance proactively a general form of cognitive control.

articles_hidden.title: Translational neuroscience in psychoeducation: Mapping nonmotor circuitry to clinical management in movement disorders
articles_hidden.authors: Behzad Elahi
articles_hidden.abstract:
Non-motor symptoms (NMS) affect nearly all patients with Parkinson’s disease (PD)
and related movement disorders, with a mean of roughly 8–10 discrete symptoms per
individual. Their effect on quality of life often exceeds that of motor features, yet
NMS remain under-recognized and undertreated, partly because patients and caregivers lack a working model of why these symptoms arise in a “movement” disease.
This chapter applies neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE) to that gap and
positions it relative to conventional psychoeducation, health communication, and behavioral science. We propose the Map-Normalize-Differentiate-Navigate (MNDN)
workflow as a movement-disorders-specific implementation of the NIPE framework
described in Chapter 1 of this volume. MNDN is a clinical proposal, not a validated
protocol: its components are specified so that it can be tested, but its effects on patient outcomes have not been evaluated. Drawing on the tripartite cortico-basal ganglia-thalamocortical loop model and multi-transmitter degeneration, we provide modules for seven high-yield NMS: apathy, anxiety, executive dysfunction, REM sleep
behavior disorder, neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, psychosis, and fatigue. Each
module summarizes the neural systems implicated, at the level of certainty the evidence supports, together with common misattributions, reversible contributors that
must be excluded, management options and their limits, and patient and caregiver
handout content. We describe delivery formats from 3 to 5 min “micro-NIPE” sessions in routine visits to group and telehealth programs, specify the minimum components, provider competencies, dose, fidelity criteria, and proximal outcomes needed
to test MNDN, and examine the ethical risks of neurobiological framing (determinism, oversimplification, over-attribution, and false reassurance), with particular attention to prognostic counseling in REM sleep behavior disorder. NIPE in movement
disorders is designed to reduce self-blame, support accurate symptom attribution, and
improve collaborative management. Whether it does so is an empirical question that
this chapter aims to make answerable.

articles_hidden.title: Psychedelics, spirituality and drug policy: Harm reduction without compulsory medicalisation
articles_hidden.authors: Baptiste Fauvel
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychedelic experiences can be meaningful and beneficial, including outside clinical treatment. They can also leave people distressed or vulnerable. Spiritual interpretations of these experiences therefore raise a practical question for drug policy: how can people be protected while preserving legitimate uses beyond psychiatry? Drawing on selected human studies and ethical and policy scholarship, this Commentary examines naturalistic benefits, mystical experiences, and concerns about spiritual bypassing and spiritual emergency, whose definitions and empirical support remain uneven. We argue that uncertainty about these risks calls for prevention and proportionate safeguards, but does not, by itself, justify restricting access to psychiatric treatment. We propose four priorities across clinical, community, and religious settings: meaningful consent, protection against exploitation, accessible support after use, and follow-up that records difficulties as well as benefits. Particular attention should be paid to interpretive autonomy: people's freedom to understand and reconsider their experiences without pressure to adopt a provider's beliefs. We claim that the notions of cognitive liberty and freedom of religion or belief strengthen the importance of scrutinising unnecessary restrictions, while retaining duties to prevent coercion and harm. We propose that policy assessment should also include harms associated with prohibition. The aim is to protect people during potentially valuable but vulnerable experiences, including those who seek meaning or well-being without a psychiatric diagnosis.

articles_hidden.title: Multi-Dimensional Reading Anxiety in Adolescence
articles_hidden.authors: Shengyun Cui; Rachelle Margaret Johnson; Joni Huikko; Mikko Aro; Jenni Ruotsalainen; Daria Khanolainen; Minna Torppa
articles_hidden.abstract: With the global decline in adolescents’ reading skills over the decade, reading-related anxiety begins to draw increasing attention. Over time, the potential feedback loop of higher anxiety and poorer reading may block pathways to academic achievements and increase the likelihood of health problems. This study examined multi-dimensional nature of reading anxiety using a sample of 654 Finnish students in Grades 7-9. The students self-assessed reading anxiety, reading control and values (utility, interest, and importance values), and reading frequency of traditional texts (e.g., book, magazine, newspaper) and digital texts (e.g., social media contents). First, confirmatory factor analysis suggested three components of reading anxiety across genders and grades, i.e., physiological and affective, cognitive, and motivational reading anxiety. Second, latent (hierarchical) regressions and difference testing further supported differences among the reading anxiety components. Lower reading control and higher reading values were associated with higher reading anxiety. Reading anxiety was also associated with reading frequency. However, cognitive reading anxiety appeared to be an essential component in terms of the overall stronger associations with reading control, values, and traditional texts reading frequency. Furthermore, reading anxiety and reading frequency association direction were variable. More frequent traditional reading was associated with higher cognitive reading anxiety, but lower physiological and affective reading anxiety (among girls) and motivational reading anxiety. More frequent digital reading was related to higher motivational reading anxiety (among boys). The findings are practically meaningful for supporting identification and regulation of reading anxiety and in turn promoting reading engagement and skills and well-being among young people.

articles_hidden.title: Impaired Updating and Maintenance of Latent Structural Associations Underlie Cognitive Inflexibility along an Obsessive–Compulsive Dimension
articles_hidden.authors: Georgios Tertikas; Nadescha Trudel; Tricia Xing Fang Seow; Miriam Klein-Flugge; Tobias U. Hauser
articles_hidden.abstract: Impaired cognitive flexibility, the ability to form and update latent structural associations, is a hallmark of psychiatric conditions such as obsessive-compulsive (OC) disorder, yet its underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Using a novel structural inference task, we dissociated three candidate mechanisms: (i) initial acquisition of associative structures, (ii) belief updating following structural changes, and (iii) inference about unobserved associations. In a large general-population sample (N=313), transdiagnostically characterised OC symptoms were linked to impaired updating following structural change and reduced generalisation to unobserved associations, whilst initial learning remained intact. Using fMRI (N=51), we found this was driven by overrepresenting structurally irrelevant associations in medial orbitofrontal cortex, and impaired formation of novel latent associations in posterior hippocampus. These findings reveal that OC-related cognitive inflexibility is grounded in dissociable fronto-hippocampal representational failures that impair structural model revision, rather than the capacity to acquire latent associations in the first place.

articles_hidden.title: Expanding the Multimodal Framework of Workplace Ostracism: Integrating Linguistic Ostracism as a Distinct Modality
articles_hidden.authors: John Fiset
articles_hidden.abstract: While research on workplace ostracism has largely focused on social, physical, and cyber modalities, emerging scholarship highlights linguistic ostracism as a distinct and under-recognized modality. It presents unique complexities due to its high attributional ambiguity, generally non-purposeful nature, and the requirement that a subgroup of two or more individuals speak a shared language unfamiliar to the target. This chapter proposes a multimodal perspective on workplace ostracism by situating linguistic ostracism alongside social, physical, and cyber modalities. Through a comparative analysis of these four modalities, the chapter identifies both shared aspects and key points of divergence. It also considers how they may interact, potentially amplifying their impact when they co-occur. By positioning linguistic ostracism as a complementary and essential form, the chapter aims to expand current theoretical frameworks and underscore the value of a multimodal approach to understanding workplace ostracism, particularly in linguistically and culturally diverse work environments.

articles_hidden.title: The Role of Prior Knowledge in Epistemic Curiosity Across Adulthood
articles_hidden.authors: Mats Abrahamse; Alexandr Ten; Kou Murayama; Michiko Sakaki
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent studies suggest that older adults maintain high levels of state curiosity when presented with epistemic materials, despite age-related declines in personality traits related to curiosity. We hypothesized that this age-related preservation in state curiosity is explained by older adults’ rich prior knowledge, given that knowledge acts as a key driver of state curiosity across the adult lifespan. To test this idea, we conducted two experiments that examined older and younger adults’ curiosity to learn the answers to questions in low- and high-knowledge domains. Experiment 1 (N = 216) used learning materials characterized by large population-level differences in prior knowledge, but limited variation across age groups. The results showed that prior knowledge substantially affects state curiosity, irrespective of age, while the effect of age on state curiosity was minimal. Experiment 2 (N = 216) explicitly accounted for age differences in knowledge by orthogonalizing the effects of knowledge and age. We found that relative to younger adults, older adults experienced stronger curiosity for high-knowledge domains, whereas in other domains where younger adults were more knowledgeable, older adults experienced weaker curiosity relative to younger adults. Such age-related differences in curiosity were mediated by age-related differences in knowledge. These findings point to the important role of prior knowledge in curiosity across younger and older adults, extending theoretical notions on curiosity. Our results also suggest that previously observed age differences in state curiosity might be partly attributable to age-related differences in knowledge.

articles_hidden.title: Repetition bias in self-directed learning
articles_hidden.authors: Alexandr Ten; Michiko Sakaki; Kou Murayama
articles_hidden.abstract:
Self-directed learning is a major part of individual knowledge formation. People often autonomously organize their own learning into ”blocks”: they practice a certain task for some continuous stretch of time, then switch to another task for another period of time, and so on. Yet current models of intrinsic motivation highlighting epistemic factors such as novelty, competence, and learning progress make various predictions about the extent to which learners block, as opposed to interleaving, their practice. In this study, we demonstrate that people tend to block in a multi-task setting where existing models of intrinsic motivation based on epistemic factors make ambiguous predictions. We show that while epistemic factors can partially explain blocking, a
simple repetition bias substantially improves our ability to predict choices.

articles_hidden.title: Maternal Stress and Mother-Child Interaction Dynamics: The Roles of Child Age and Maternal Emotion Regulation
articles_hidden.authors: Julia Folz; Trinh Nguyen; Stefanie Hoehl; Vanessa Anna van Ast; Milica Nikolic
articles_hidden.abstract: Caregivers often face stressful multi-tasking situations in which household- or work-related tasks compete with engaging with their young child. Caregivers’ experiences of stress can affect how they interact with their children and may also be transmitted to the child. This “stress contagion” may be particularly pronounced with caregivers who have difficulties in regulating stress responses. In the current study, we examined how inducing stress in 62 mothers shaped the dyadic interaction (expression of facial affect and cardiovascular activity) with their 6-38 months-old children, and how stress-induced changes varied depending on self-reported maternal emotion regulation difficulties and child age. Mothers’ and children’s positive and negative facial affect, inter-beat intervals (IBIs) and respiratory sinus arrhythmia (RSA), as well as synchrony in each measure, were compared between two-minute face-to-face interactions before and after a stress induction in the mother (pre- and post-stress). Maternal stress impacted the dyad differently depending on the child’s age. In interactions with younger children, both mothers and children showed less positive facial expressions and were less synchronized in their expressions post- versus pre-stress. Older children, in contrast, showed stronger physiological arousal (i.e., decrease in IBIs and RSA), but more positive facial expressions post-stress. In addition, mothers with more emotion regulation difficulties expressed more negative affect, and their heart rates were less synchronized with their children’s post- versus pre-stress. Both child age and mothers’ regulatory abilities are thus shaping the impact of acute maternal stress on mother-child interaction quality and should be considered in interventions on parental stress

articles_hidden.title: Is Change in Motivation in College a Normative Calibration Process or an Early Warning Sign?
articles_hidden.authors: Luise von Keyserlingk; Hye Rin Lee; Charlott Rubach; Hanna Gaspard; Gabe Avakian Orona; Jutta Heckhausen; Jacquelynne S Eccles
articles_hidden.abstract: Motivation often declines at the beginning of college. Such declines may reflect adaptive calibration to new academic demands or signal emerging academic risk. This study examined how course-specific expectancies of success, utility value, and cost changed within and across courses in the first college year, how these changes were related to course difficulty and performance feedback, and whether they predicted performance and persistence. Participants were 942 first-year students at one U.S. university. In each of three quarters of their freshman year, students reported their motivation three times per course in two personally salient courses. Latent change score models showed that expectancies and utility value declined from the beginning to the middle of courses and then stabilized or recovered. Contrary to predictions, perceived cost declined early and remained stable thereafter. These patterns recurred across quarters, although students began later quarters with lower expectancies and utility values. Motivation also varied by course context: students reported lower expectancies and utility values and higher cost in more difficult courses than in perceived important courses. Higher midterm grades predicted smaller decreases in expectancies and utility value and larger decreases in cost, consistent with motivational recalibration following performance feedback. Higher motivational levels and smaller decreases in expectancies and utility value predicted stronger intentions to remain in the major, but they did not consistently predict final course grades or actual major change. Findings suggest that first-year motivational change is a repeated, situated calibration that may become concerning when lower motivational baselines accumulate across courses and over time.

articles_hidden.title: Everyone else does it? Self-reported and perceived questionable research practices in music psychology
articles_hidden.authors: Andrew Danso; Tuomas Eerola
articles_hidden.abstract: Questionable research practices (QRPs) may inflate false-positive rates and have been surveyed in psychology, ecology, and education, but not in music psychology. In a survey, 198 researchers who had authored empirical music-psychology work reported how often they had used 22 practices and estimated how many colleagues had used each. Three quarters (75.1%) reported at least one of the 18 practices bearing on false-positive risk, and 82.8% at least one of all 22. The most common were citing irrelevant work to satisfy a reviewer (46.9%) and selecting the most favourable analysis after seeing the results (43.5%). Respondents estimated that colleagues used 20 of the 22 practices more than they did themselves, but this gap is largely produced by the response scale in the survey and is not evidence of under-reporting. Researchers who thought practices were more widespread reported more of them between persons (OR = 2.16, 95% CI [1.74, 2.68]) and within them (OR = 2.62, [2.32, 2.96]), consistent with false consensus as well as descriptive norms. Music-specific practices were reported less often than reporting and analysis practices, though this depended partly on item wording and on whether a practice applied at all. Career stage showed no detectable association with admissions. Researchers reporting more open research practices reported more QRPs, not fewer (OR = 1.28, [1.14, 1.44]), which may indicate differences in disclosure as much as in behaviour. These results provide a first baseline for the field.

articles_hidden.title: Measuring Cognitive Noise: Separating Signal Strength from Random Fluctuations in Evidence Accumulation
articles_hidden.authors: andreas voss
articles_hidden.abstract: The diffusion model decomposes choices and response times into parameters for the speed of information uptake (drift rate), the information required for a decision (boundary separation), decision bias (starting point), and extra-decisional processes (nondecision time). A further parameter, the diffusion coefficient s, scales the random variability of accumulation within a trial. Because the likelihood is invariant to a joint rescaling of drift, boundaries, and s, this parameter is conventionally fixed and treated as a meaningless scaling constant. I argue that this convention implicitly assumes that all persons and conditions share the same amount of cognitive noise, and that it renders drift and boundary effects ambiguous, because only the ratios of signal and boundary to noise are identified. I propose two approaches that separate signal strength and noise by adding one psychologically motivated assumption. The Bounded Drift approach links stimulus information to drift rate through a psychophysical function and fixes the maximum drift at a common value. The Random Walk approach assumes that evidence arrives in discrete samples of constant size at an individual rate, so that sampling determines both drift and noise. Both models were implemented with amortized Bayesian inference in BayesFlow, and simulations show satisfactory recovery and calibration of the noise parameters. In a pilot study with five younger and five older adults, noise estimates converged over both approaches (r = .74). I discuss cognitive noise as a measurable individual difference and outline a validation program.

articles_hidden.title: Unveiling the Hidden Barrier: A Scoping Review of Approach Anxiety in Male Dating Behavior
