articles_hidden.authors: Benjamin Storbeck; Bertus F. Jeronimus
articles_hidden.abstract: Approach anxiety (AA) describes a fear or intense nervousness about approaching or initiating social and especially dating interactions, where approach and avoidance goals collide. We review literature on AA in the context of human dating behavior to (a) evaluate the scientific status of AA as a distinct psychological concept and construct and (b) identify key associations with and causes of AA. Our scoping review identified zero studies of AA specifically, despite the widespread recognition of AA in popular media and self-help platforms, although we identified 83 studies of psychological dynamics during the initial phase of social interaction. Academic literature seems to ignore AA despite the many young men who say AA is a major problem. We provide a AA construct clarification and evidence integration of studies of youth social interaction dynamics which describe social or dating anxiety, fear of rejection, or heterosocial competence. AA describes a complex interplay of sex differences, attachment styles, cultural expectations, and individual psychological factors. We present a Multilevel Courtship Inhibition Framework (MCIF) of AA that connects social skill deficits and psychological challenges with potential evolutionary, sociocultural, and psychological underpinnings, to help catalyze academic AA research.

articles_hidden.title: Knowing the Rules of the Game: Political Knowledge as a Buffer Against National Narcissism and Anti-Democratic Sentiment
articles_hidden.authors: Piotr Michalski; Marta Marchlewska; Adam Karakula
articles_hidden.abstract: Different forms of political knowledge may play distinct roles in shaping citizens’ commitment to democracy. We focused on two facets: knowledge about the rules of the game (understanding of democratic principles and institutional structures) and current political knowledge (awareness of ongoing political events and actors). We proposed that knowledge about the rules of the game, in particular, may serve as a psychological resource that buffers against anti-democratic sentiments. In both studies, knowledge about the rules of the game was associated with more pro-democratic attitudes (higher support for democracy, lower dictatorship endorsement, and lower conspiracy beliefs). These associations were explained by lower national narcissism, a defensive belief in the nation’s unrecognized greatness. Study 2 extended this model by examining citizens’ evaluations of their country’s democratic quality as an additional indirect-effect variable. A serial pathway emerged: greater knowledge about the rules of the game was linked to lower national narcissism, which was associated with more positive evaluations of the country’s democracy, and in turn with stronger pro-democratic orientations. Current political knowledge, in contrast, showed a more ambivalent pattern. It related to anti-democratic sentiments via higher national narcissism, but also showed protective associations through stronger national identification. Together, these findings suggest that not all political knowledge plays the same role in sustaining democracy—structural understanding of democratic systems emerges as a particularly meaningful civic resource.

articles_hidden.title: Caught Between Two Worlds: The role of Bicultural Identity Conflict in the Longitudinal Effects of Perceived Discrimination on Migrants’ Life Satisfaction and  Health
articles_hidden.authors: Maximilian Schmidt; Christina Bauer; Gerald Echterhoff; Marco Marinucci
articles_hidden.abstract: Both forced and voluntary migration are incisive life events that prompt acculturation processes fundamental for the adaptation in the host society, including the formation of a second cultural identity. One of the major challenges to the acculturation process is the discrimination by the host national groups. Previous research showed that it can both undermine the development of integrated bicultural identities and impact migrants’ well-being in many ways. However, previous research investigating this process only relied on correlational methods. Our study tests how dynamics between discrimination, bicultural identity, well-being, and health evolve over time, hypothesizing a longitudinal effect of discrimination on bicultural identity conflict as one important process that may link perceived discrimination with lower life satisfaction and health. We conducted a secondary data analysis of longitudinal data with N = 285 migrants in integration courses in Germany (24,4% forced) including two time points spanning six months. The research highlights how the perception of discrimination can be a key risk factor that undermines the development of harmonious bicultural identity over time, with key detrimental repercussions for migrants’ adaptation, life satisfaction and  health.

articles_hidden.title: Avoiding the worst leaders is more important than getting the best
articles_hidden.authors: Hallgeir Sjåstad; Jareef Martuza; Jay Joseph Van Bavel
articles_hidden.abstract: Society and organizations invest heavily in selecting the best leaders 1, and existing research shows a positivity bias by focusing on the bright side of leadership 2–4. Yet, according to Popper 5, the central question of institutional design is not who should rule, but how to prevent bad leaders from doing too much damage. This raises the question of which approach is more consistent with human psychology: Aim for the best leaders, or avoid the worst? We provide robust evidence for an “avoid-the-worst” principle in human leadership preferences. Although text analyses indicated that the top 100 business schools emphasize good leadership far more than the prevention of bad leadership, actual employee experiences from 9.9 million Glassdoor reviews show that people mentioned their leader 70% more often in the negative than positive section, and negative leader mentions predicted company ratings 1.5 times more strongly. Providing causal evidence, five high-powered experiments across 40 countries (N = 51,433) revealed that people were more willing to sacrifice time and money to avoid a bad leader than obtaining a good leader—across morality and competence, hypothetical and incentivized choice, ideology and culture. People care more about avoiding the worst leaders than getting the best.

articles_hidden.title: AI-Powered Prevention and Early Intervention for Stress, Depression, and Anxiety: A Randomized Clinical Trial
articles_hidden.authors: Julie Youko Anne Cachia; Xuan Zhao; Wenxi Pu; Chi Liao; merel Keijsers; Julian De Freitas; Rebecca Fortgang
articles_hidden.abstract: Randomized evidence for purpose-built generative AI mental health support remains limited. In this preregistered trial, 1,137 unscreened university students were assigned to 6 weeks of a generative AI-powered mobile intervention (“Flourish”) or care as usual. Across the full sample, Flourish produced more favorable trajectories for perceived stress (β = −0.03, p = 0.010), depressive symptoms (β = −0.03, p = 0.006), and anxiety symptoms (β = −0.04, p = 0.001). Reduced perceived stress emerged as a potential pathway to symptom improvement. To our knowledge, this is the first trial supporting purpose-built, safety-first generative AI for mental health prevention and early intervention in an unscreened population.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond reflective verbal self-reports: Development and validation of the Meditation Pictographic Inventory (MPI) through a multi-source framework
articles_hidden.authors: Ylenia D'elia; Oscar Lecuona; Rocío Herrero; ROSA MARIA BAÑOS RIVERA; Maja Wrzesien; Ausiàs Cebolla
articles_hidden.abstract: Single-item measures are increasingly used to capture constructs that are impractical to assess with multi-item scales, yet their reliability is difficult to estimate and validity evidence is rarely combined across sources. Meditation-related states, which are embodied and often hard to verbalize, illustrate this challenge. The study followed two phases. Phase 1 aimed to develop and refine the pictographic items through qualitative interviews with 10 meditation experts. Phase 2 aimed to validate the MPI. Adults (N = 378) from the general population were randomized to one of four conditions: three brief meditation practices (counting breath, loving-kindness, decentering) or an active control. Validity evidence covered content, response processes, sensitivity to change, relations with other variables, incremental prediction, and internal structure via network analysis at pre- and post-meditation. Reliability was examined through test-retest, criterion-based, and generalizability analyses. However, nine items were sensitive to meditation effects, including both general (e.g., body boundaries) and practice-specific effects (e.g., warmth after loving-kindness). Items correlated with related self-reports as expected and predicted post-meditation outcomes, but not beyond baseline levels. Single-item reliability was modest. Positive and negative cluster scores showed adequate generalizability, whereas time- and self-related items require further revision. The study was preregistered, the MPI and all materials are openly available, and the framework offers a template for validating other single item inventories.

articles_hidden.title: “Maybe I don’t wanna be the bad guy”;  Young Children’s Resistance to Immoral Actions
articles_hidden.authors: Anna Sofia Sofia Caruso; Thalia R Goldstein
articles_hidden.abstract: Children are often thought to engage in imagination freely, but research has found they show boundaries in their play. However, when and how children show limits to moral permissiveness specifically within their pretense is unknown. We conducted two studies to investigate how and when children display moral boundaries and Imaginative Resistance during imaginative activities. Study 1 tested 60 children (aged 4-6) with scenarios differing on moral valence (moral or immoral) and agent (self or other) and asked for evaluations of immoral actions in different contexts. Study 2, a large online replication of study 1 (N = 152; aged 4-7) suggested a developmental trajectory of more Imaginative Resistance with age. Across both studies, children resisted engagement in immoral play, however, they were more morally permissible in pretend over real contexts. Thus, Imaginative Resistance follows a developmental trajectory, showing possibilities for malleable moral engagement and intervention opportunities on moral judgements.

articles_hidden.title: A Critical Review of Caregiver Report Measures of Autistic Traits in Children (4 to 12 years): Considerations for Research and Clinical Practice
articles_hidden.authors: Georgia Horsburgh; Iliana Magiati; Murray Maybery; Lauren J Taylor; Serena J Cribb; Michael C W English
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Selecting an appropriate questionnaire to measure autistic traits in children for research or clinical practice requires considering several factors. These include the validity of the questionnaire’s structure, the questionnaire’s sensitivity and specificity, the extent to which autistic traits are represented (e.g., whether all diagnostic sub-criteria are adequately represented), the clarity and respectfulness of item wording, and inclusive research practices used during questionnaire development. To provide clinicians and researchers information on the most sensitive, specific, and contemporary measures for identifying and assessing autistic traits, we conducted a review of existing caregiver-report questionnaires for measuring autistic traits in children aged 4-12 years.
Method: Ten questionnaires were identified for inclusion. For each included questionnaire, targeted searches were conducted in the form of forward citation searches to identify peer-reviewed studies reporting on the instrument’s development or subsequent psychometric evaluation (factor or component analysis, sensitivity, specificity). 
Results: Overall, there was marked variability in the extent to which questionnaires assess autistic traits across diagnostic sub-criteria, as well as in their sensitivity and specificity for differentiating autism from various other groups. Several questionnaires lacked psychometric support for their proposed structure. Respectfulness and clarity of item wording could be improved in most questionnaires. Autism community input during questionnaire development was typically limited or absent. Of note, the recently developed Autism Symptom Dimensions Questionnaire stood out as a promising freely available measure. 
Discussion: Developers of new questionnaires should use inclusive research practices, write items using clear and respectful language, ensure adequate psychometric properties, and aim to include items from all diagnostic sub-criteria.

articles_hidden.title: Prioritization of Perceptual Decisions
articles_hidden.authors: Daniel R. Little; Luke Russell; Peizhao Xie; Ruby Steinberg; Asha Bartlett; Ami Eidels
articles_hidden.abstract: Scheduling theory provides optimal policies for allocating limited resources to multiple tasks over time. However, little research has examined how cognitive mechanisms perform relative to these optimal policies. We introduce a novel experimental paradigm to study human scheduling decisions using a set of perceptual tasks (random dot kinematograms, RDKs) that vary in difficulty. A foundational question in this paradigm is how optimal prioritization depends on the representation of task factors. Participants selected and completed RDKs one at a time, with the goal of completing as many as possible before a deadline. In Experiment 1 (collected in 2020), RDK difficulty was explicitly labeled. Participants showed near-optimal scheduling, selecting easier tasks first, especially under time pressure. In Experiment 2 (collected in 2022), difficulty had to be inferred from dynamic RDK displays. This resulted in less optimal scheduling, closer to random selection. In Experiment 3 (collected in 2026), we removed observation time from the selection and completion time by limiting the time window in which participants could view the moving RDKs. Across increasing time windows from 200 to 1600 ms, we showed that the optimality of the resulting schedule grew with increasing observation time. We develop a cognitive model of scheduling based on the Plackett-Luce model of ranked preferences. The model captures key differences between experiments in terms of the strength parameters associated with each difficulty level. Our paradigm and modeling approach provide a foundation for studying human scheduling across a range of task types and goals.

articles_hidden.title: Humans and Large Language Models Infer a Multidimensional Structure of Moral Motivation
articles_hidden.authors: Paul McKee; Andrew James; Breanna K. Nguyen; Madison Monroe-Mohajerin; Scott A. Huettel; Walter Sinnott-Armstrong
articles_hidden.abstract: Moral evaluation depends not only on what people do, but on why observers believe they acted as they did. Human participants (N = 1,031) and 23 frontier LLMs evaluated 344 real-world moral narratives using identical procedures. All four motivational dimensions were inferred frequently in both populations and exhibited structured patterns of co-occurrence. Human observers clustered antisocial motivations (Approach Bad and Avoid Good) more strongly than prosocial motivations, whereas LLMs exhibited the opposite pattern. Across all evaluative outcomes, inferred motivations systematically predicted judgments of rightness, wrongness, praiseworthiness, and blameworthiness. Supervised machine learning analyses further demonstrated that the complete four-dimensional representation consistently outperformed every reduced two-dimensional alternative, indicating that each motivational dimension contributed unique predictive information. Although LLMs broadly recovered the multidimensional structure observed in humans, they inferred antisocial motivations less frequently, concentrated those attributions within fewer narratives, and produced systematically compressed response distributions characterized by lower variance and entropy. Together, these findings suggest that moral motivation is best understood as a multidimensional representational system and that representational richness provides a useful framework for evaluating both human moral cognition and its approximation by artificial systems.

articles_hidden.title: Passing the Wrong Test: Model Size and Discriminant Validity in LLM-Based Psychological Assessment
articles_hidden.authors: Yosef Sokol; Amar D. Mandavia; Jaclyn C. Kearns
articles_hidden.abstract: Validation studies of zero-shot language-model scoring of psychological interviews often rely primarily on a single convergent correlation with a questionnaire to establish validity. However, a bivariate correlation cannot reveal whether a model lacks discriminant validity, agrees poorly in absolute terms, produces non-random missing scores, or scores inconsistently. The models scored the same sets of clinical interviews (Study 1: suicide recovery, n = 149; Study 2: future self-continuity, n = 164) across 52 configurations. However, the standard open-weight models tested achieve only about three-quarters of frontier convergent validity, with 11-fold greater mean absolute bias, more format failures, and lower repeatability in Study 1. In Study 2, standard open models (≤ 27B) are as strongly correlated with a closely related construct (suicide recovery) as with the target (mean difference −0.014), although they correlate less strongly with a distal neighbor (life satisfaction). All six frontier generations correlate more strongly with the target than with either neighbor (mean difference from recovery +0.117). On a local workstation, Gemma 4 31B is within the frontier range on all discriminant validity indices, outperforming its similar-sized predecessor. Llama 3.3 70B shows no greater discriminant validity than Gemma 4 31B, suggesting that discriminant validity is a function of release, not parameter count alone. Based on these findings, we suggest a minimum validation standard across five domains.

articles_hidden.title: Retrospective harmonization of neuropsychiatric questionnaires in a large multi-site research consortium using expert mappings and semantic textual similarity
articles_hidden.authors: Julia-Katharina Pfarr; Eva van Heese; Joshua Curtiss; Max A. Laansma; Emile d'Angremont; Conor Owens-Walton; Auwal Abdullahi; Manon Auffret; Yun Jung Bae; Bhupender Kumar Bajaj
articles_hidden.abstract: Differences between clinical questionnaires limit the pooling of symptom data across studies, particularly when participants have completed different instruments. This semantic, dimensional harmonization approach supports retrospective pooling of heterogeneous questionnaire data and offers a practical and systematic path toward mega-analyses on retrospective datasets.

articles_hidden.title: A novel method for detecting the onset of experimental effects in visual world eye-tracking
articles_hidden.authors: João Veríssimo; Sol Lago
articles_hidden.abstract: Determining the onset of experimental effects in timeseries data is central to psycholinguistics, because onset timing constrains theories about when different types of linguistic information become available during language processing. Several onset detection methods have been proposed for the visual world paradigm. An increasingly adopted approach is the bootstrap-based method of Stone, Lago, and Schad (2021), but its accuracy in recovering underlying onset values has not yet been formally evaluated. We address this gap with two simulation studies and propose a novel onset detection method based on generalised additive mixed models (GAMMs) and posterior simulation. This method integrates timecourse modelling with onset estimation and supports the direct comparison of onset times across experimental conditions and participant groups. Our simulations showed that the GAMM-based method produced less biased and more accurate onset estimates than the bootstrap-based method, as well as generally better confidence interval coverage. Although both methods tended to estimate onsets later than their underlying values, the delays were smaller for the GAMM-based method. Differences in curve steepness could also produce spurious significant differences between estimated onsets, but these occurred less frequently with the GAMM-based method. We demonstrate the practical application of the GAMM-based method by reanalysing two published visual world datasets and provide a user-friendly R package to facilitate its adoption. By enabling more accurate estimation of effect timing in the visual world paradigm, our method can contribute to advancing theories of prediction and language comprehension.

articles_hidden.title: Retinal biomarkers and dementia risk: A review of evidence across the 14 Lancet modifiable risk factors for dementia
articles_hidden.authors: Ashleigh Barrett-Young
articles_hidden.abstract: As the only central nervous system tissue that can be directly imaged non-invasively using widely available technology, the retina offers a uniquely accessible window into the brain. Quantitative retinal measures can be derived at scale and have been associated with mechanistic processes in the brain and throughout the body, positioning retinal biomarkers as promising tools for dementia prevention and intervention research. Evidence indicates that several retinal biomarkers can distinguish individuals with Alzheimer’s disease (AD) from cognitively healthy controls; however, it remains unclear whether these markers reflect preclinical AD-specific pathology or broader profiles of dementia risk, particularly in the earliest stages of disease. This review synthesises current evidence on retinal microvascular and neuronal morphological biomarkers and their associations with 14 modifiable dementia risk factors identified by the Lancet Commission on dementia. Robust evidence indicates that retinal biomarkers are influenced by vascular and metabolic risks, specifically hypertension and diabetes. However, associations with other modifiable risk factors, including social isolation, lower educational attainment, hearing loss, smoking, air pollution, and traumatic brain injury, are sparse or absent. Critical research gaps persist regarding how, when, and for whom the retina reflects vascular and metabolic risk factors, and whether non-biological risk factors, such as social isolation and educational attainment, are better understood as independent or confounding variables than as direct biological determinants of retinal biomarkers. Clarifying these associations is essential to establish retinal biomarkers as scalable, non-invasive indicators of dementia risk and to support their integration into targeted risk stratification, early detection, and preventive intervention studies.

articles_hidden.title: Emotional Well-Being Among Adults with Comorbid Alcohol and Cannabis Use Disorders: Evidence from the COGA Lifespan Study
articles_hidden.authors: Fatima Hijazi; Jiawen Zhao; Megan Cooke; Sally I Kuo; Kathleen Bucholz; Grace Chan; Genevieve Fullerton Dash; Fanghong Dong; Christina Elizabeth Garasky; Chella Kamarajan
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background. Alcohol use disorder (AUD) and cannabis use disorder (CUD) are often comorbid. Concurrent or simultaneous use of alcohol and cannabis is associated with poorer mental health outcomes in cross-sectional studies. Here, we examined whether lifetime history of comorbid AUD and CUD is associated with emotional well-being, above and beyond current substance use and lifetime major depression. 
Methods. Participants were 1,393 adults from the Collaborative Study on the Genetics of Alcohol Lifespan assessment (Mage= 52.0, 59.7% female). Emotional well-being was assessed across six domains from the NIH Toolbox Emotion Battery: loneliness, perceived stress, negative affect, social satisfaction, psychological well-being, and self-efficacy. Associations between lifetime diagnostic group (comorbid AUD + CUD, AUD without CUD, CUD without AUD, or neither disorder) and emotional well-being outcomes were assessed using multivariate linear regression. Covariates included age, sex, and past-year nicotine, cannabis, and alcohol use. Sensitivity analyses adjusted for lifetime major depressive disorder.
Results. Individuals with comorbid lifetime AUD + CUD reported higher loneliness, perceived stress, and negative affect, and lower social satisfaction, psychological well-being, and self-efficacy compared to other groups. Individuals with lifetime AUD without CUD or CUD without AUD generally resembled those with neither disorder across several emotional well-being domains, though those in the AUD without CUD group reported greater negative affect and lower social satisfaction and psychological well-being than the group with neither disorder. 
Conclusions. A lifetime history of comorbid AUD and CUD is associated with diminished emotional well-being, underscoring the need for additional psychosocial supports to address these challenges in this population.

articles_hidden.title: Strategy-mediated cue combination in navigation
articles_hidden.authors: Yu Karen Du; weimin mou; Jennifer Sutton; Blake Edward Butler
articles_hidden.abstract: Cue combination and competition in navigation have been observed among various spatial cues, yet it remains unclear whether the decision to combine cues is driven by the uncertainties of individual cues or by strategy-level competition. To address this, we examined whether compound or single cue learning experience can influence the selection of cue combination or competition. Participants learned target locations in a virtual environment with two landmarks and were assigned to either the compound learning group (who encoded the target with both landmarks) or the single learning group (who learned from one landmark at a time). In the testing phase, participants recalled the target location under single-cue, compound, and landmark-shift (conflict) conditions. In compound tests, both groups showed lower variances than in single-cue tests, indicating optimal cue combination based on single-cue uncertainties. In shift tests, however, despite optimal cue weights, no variance reduction was observed, and the variances were inconsistent with both cue combination and competition models. Using a maximum likelihood estimation approach, we estimated the probability of using the combination strategy and found that learning experience systematically modulated this probability: The majority of the compound learning group showed high probabilities of combination, whereas the single learning group showed large individual differences. AIC model comparisons indicate that our strategy selection model, which incorporates the estimated probability of combination, provided a better fit to the observed data than pure combination or competition models, especially in shift tests. These results support the strategy-mediated account, suggesting a potential decision-making process in cue combination.

articles_hidden.title: Postcolonial English Exposure and the Visual Mental Timeline
articles_hidden.authors: Ibrahim Shahid
articles_hidden.abstract: The spatial-temporal association of response codes (STEARC) effect describes faster responses when past-related stimuli map onto the left and future-related stimuli map onto the right. This exploratory study asked whether an English-official-language or colonial-history background is associated with a smaller STEARC effect, and whether any such association is specific to the visual modality. Trial-level data came from 96 participants. An attention check retained 70 participants and 135 participant-by-modality scores. STEARC was the mean response time (RT) of incongruent trials minus that of congruent trials, computed with a fixed left-to-right mapping for every participant. A mixed model showed a colonial history by modality interaction, F(1, 130) = 8.64, p = .004, pFDR = .012. The visual contrast was −515 ms, 95% CI [−854, −176]. After adjustment for reading direction the contrast was −391 ms, 95% CI [−846, 64], p = .091, and the Bayes factor was inconclusive (BF01 = 1.78). Colonial history and reading direction overlapped strongly (φ = .59), and 17 of the 26 participants with a colonial history read right to left. Resampling checks supported the unadjusted contrast but not clearly the adjusted contrast, and the interaction did not reach significance without the attention filter. The results are consistent with, but do not establish, an influence of postcolonial English exposure on the visual mental timeline. We treat them as a hypothesis for a design in which colonial history and reading direction are crossed, and we give sample sizes for that design.

articles_hidden.title: Blind-spot maps: auditing what a structural equation model’s design could not have detected
articles_hidden.authors: Marek Deja
articles_hidden.abstract: A structural equation model can fit its data even when the design had little chance of detecting substantively relevant alternatives. A blind-spot map enumerates single-parameter alternatives to a fitted model, applies each at a standardized magnitude that holds implied variances fixed, and reports the probability that a stated decision rule would flag the model if the alternative were true, beside the probability that the same rule flags a correctly specified model. Analytic detection from the noncentral chi-square is paired with a simulated path that measures each rule’s finite-sample size, and equivalence that follows from a saturated latent structure is certified by proof instead of by a numerical threshold. In ten published designs with N from 20 to 2,566, 2,035 alternatives are detectable, and all 177 admissible directed-path and latent-covariance alternatives are certified equivalent, so the fits test only the measurement structure. Median detection under the likelihood-ratio test rises from .071 at N = 20 to .996 at N = 2,566, and the largest design still has three blind spots, residual correlations of 0.3 detected at most 9.6 percent of the time against a size of 5.8 percent. The RMSEA > .06 rule flags 457 alternatives below .50 that the likelihood-ratio test detects above .80, and its measured size reaches .434 at N = 20. A declared block of correlated residuals among reverse-keyed items is detected with probability .998 where no single pair exceeds .520. Independent R and Julia packages generate reproducible artifacts.

articles_hidden.title: Psychological processes linking insomnia with depression and anxiety in emerging adulthood
articles_hidden.authors: Amelia Stanton; Qimin Liu; Katherine Kabel; Mingcong Tang; William A. Bauer; Rebecca Cox; Sarah Lipson; Martin Seehuus
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Insomnia is strongly associated with symptoms of depression and anxiety during emerging adulthood, yet the mechanisms underlying these relationships remain poorly understood. Numerous constructs have been proposed as potential explanatory pathways, but few have been systematically screened and independently replicated. This study applied a structured associational variable screening approach to identify and replicate candidate constructs associated with relationships connecting insomnia and depression and anxiety in emerging adults. 

Methods: Data were drawn from two independent samples of emerging adults. Study 1 (N = 333) provided exploratory analyses and Study 2 (N = 1,555) provided independent confirmation. Insomnia symptoms were assessed using the Sleep Condition Indicator (SCI) and depression and anxiety symptoms using the Depression Anxiety Stress Scales (DASS). Candidate associative variables included psychological inflexibility, emotion regulation difficulties, behavioral and experiential avoidance, maladaptive sleep-related behaviors and attitudes. Following Weems et al. (2025), candidates were evaluated using sequential analyses of zero-order associations, multivariable associations and incremental explanatory power (ΔR²), attenuation of the sleep–symptom association, equivalence under reversal of the proposed associative pathway, and moderation.

Results: In Study 1, emotion regulation difficulties, psychological inflexibility, and behavioral avoidance met screening criteria as potential path variables between insomnia and depression, while emotion regulation difficulties and psychological inflexibility met criteria as potential path variables between insomnia and anxiety. These candidate associations were replicated in Study 2. For depression, emotion regulation difficulties (ΔR² = .277), psychological inflexibility (ΔR² = .286), and behavioral avoidance (ΔR² = .122) demonstrated substantial incremental explanatory power. For anxiety, emotion regulation difficulties (ΔR² = .175) and psychological inflexibility (ΔR² = .182) met all screening criteria, with internalizing demonstrating the largest incremental contribution. Moderation models were estimated but consistently explained negligible additional variance (ΔR² ≤ .006).

Conclusions: Across exploratory and confirmatory samples, psychological inflexibility and emotion regulation difficulties emerged as consistent candidate associative variables linking insomnia with both depressive and anxiety symptoms. Behavioral avoidance additionally emerged for depression. Although the cross-sectional design precludes causal or mechanistic inference, these findings narrow a broad set of potential explanatory constructs and identify promising candidates for longitudinal and experimental research examining relationships between sleep disturbance and depression and anxiety during emerging adulthood.

articles_hidden.title: The Prevalence of Bayesian Inference, Preregistration, and Open Data in Psychology, 2004-2024
articles_hidden.authors: Julius M. Pfadt; František Bartoš; Henrik R. Godmann; Meike Waaijers; Laura Groot; Ihnwhi Heo; Lotte Mensink; Jason Nak; Jan Peter De Ruiter; Alexandra Sarafoglou
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychology has undergone substantial methodological changes in the past two decades. In ‘top-tier’ journals, human (50%) and LLM-assisted (50%) full-text coding revealed that in 2024, 26% of articles reported a Bayesian analysis, 41% included a preregistration, and 73% provided open data. In ‘mid-tier’ journals, LLM coding showed corresponding rates of 16%, 18%, and 40%. From 2004 to 2012, these practices were virtually nonexistent. Bayesian logistic growth modeling suggests further increases, although their extent remains uncertain. Mixed-effects models became more prevalent, software reporting improved, with greater use of R and less reliance on SPSS, but estimation-focused (vs. hypothesis-testing-focused) reporting showed only modest gains. Despite heterogeneity across journals, psychology articles published in 2024 differ markedly from those published only a decade earlier.

articles_hidden.title: Thinking ahead to eat less? Comparing food- versus activity-based episodic future thinking on snack consumption across two pre-registered experimental studies
articles_hidden.authors: Jennifer Gatzemeier; Laura L. Wilkinson; Menna Price; Michelle LEE
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: In our current food environment, psychosocial strategies to reduce intake and related overweight/obesity are needed. Thinking vividly about one’s personal health goal or future event (episodic future thinking; EFT) can reduce intake in the present moment. Some people think about their future food plans instead, which might be for the same day or for a few days later. As this has not been considered in previous research, the present studies aimed to investigate how EFT related factors (food-related EFTs and time between the current moment and the future event) influence snack intake with dietary restraint included as a moderator. 
Methods: Across two pre-registered experimental studies, participants were randomly allocated to either food-related EFT or control (activity-based EFT). Study 1 focused on food-related EFT for the present day, while study 2 also included food-related EFT for the next day. Intake of six different sweet and savoury snacks, and dietary restraint were assessed. 
Results: For study one, 124 (Mage=29.7±13.2, MBMI=24.8±4.9) and for study two, 187 participants (Mage=21.6±5.8, MBMI=24.0±5.1) attended the lab. There was no significant difference in food intake following either a food- or activity-based EFT task (irrespective of duration between the present moment and the future event). Overall, restraint did not moderate this relationship. 
Conclusion: While health EFT has been shown to reduce intake in the literature, this effect has not been extended to food-related EFT here. This might indicate the importance of content and delivery of EFT cues.

articles_hidden.title: Descriptive Norms, Self-Efficacy, and Avoidance of Simultaneous Alcohol–Cannabis Use and Cannabis-Impaired Driving: A Prospective Test of Social Cognitive Theory
articles_hidden.authors: Bella M. González Ponce; Fermín Fernández-Calderón; Daniel Dacosta-Sánchez; Judith Muriel Gómez; Angélica Gemio Martín
articles_hidden.abstract: Simultaneous alcohol and cannabis use (SAC) and driving under the influence of cannabis (DUIC) are prevalent risk behaviors among young adults who use cannabis. Controlling for sex, age, university status, and baseline risk behavior, higher descriptive norms and self-efficacy were associated with greater avoidance of both behaviors. Self-efficacy mediated the association between norms and avoidance of both behaviors, and neither the association between norms and self-efficacy nor the indirect association differed significantly by sex. Sex moderated only the association between norms and DUIC avoidance, which was significant among men. Normative feedback interventions highlighting peers´ avoidance could target both perceived norms and self-efficacy, especially for DUIC among men.

articles_hidden.title: Development and Validation of Team Functional Degrees of Freedom (TfDoF): An Eco-Physical Variable for Functional Collective Off-ball Movements in Football
articles_hidden.authors: Li Xiao; Daniel Carrilho; enrico serra; Nelson Caldeira; Rui J. Lopes; Duarte Araújo
articles_hidden.abstract: In football, limited research has considered both the processes underlying collective behavior and its functional outcomes, constraining its practical applicability. In this study, we developed and validated an eco-physical variable, Team Functional Degrees of Freedom (TfDoF), to quantify how off-ball players dynamically coordinate their movements with teammates, opponents, and the ball to afford functional passing opportunities for a team in football. TfDoF was developed through a “glocal” spatial framework integrating centroid dynamics, Voronoi diagrams, dynamic pitch zoning, and a rule-based degrees-of-freedom approach. Validation comprised two complementary stages. First, expert-based validation involved seven football experts who evaluated the computational framework and identified passing opportunities in 30 match clips at the instant of passing. TfDoF showed a very strong correlation with expert-perceived passing opportunities (r = .98, p < .001), while all content validity indices exceeded .86, providing preliminary evidence of its content and convergent validity. Second, performance-based validation examined the relationship between TfDoF and pass outcomes using synchronized tracking and event data from 35 Italian Serie A matches (20,531 passes). Among six machine learning algorithms, XGBoost achieved the best classification performance (AUC = 0.909). SHAP analysis identified TfDoF as the most influential predictor of pass success (FI = 1.453), providing evidence of its predictive validity. Notably, TfDoF’s contribution to pass success was non-linear, with the greatest marginal effect occurring between TfDoF values of 5 and 7. Finally, we proposed a multi-timescale analytical framework demonstrating how TfDoF can support tactical analysis and coaching practice.

articles_hidden.title: One Dance, Two Partners: Session-to-Session Therapist–Client Rating Configurations and Outcomes
articles_hidden.authors: Qiong Wu; Lenore M McWey
articles_hidden.abstract: This study identified session-level patterns of therapists’ and clients’ perceptions of the therapeutic alliance and treatment progress and examined whether these patterns were associated with client-reported outcomes. Data included 15 therapist trainees, 86 clients, and 1,035 session ratings. After each session, therapists and clients separately provided ratings, and clients rated their personal functioning and psychological symptoms. A multilevel latent class analysis identified five session patterns: “all-high” (53.3%), “bond-focused” (16.3%), “goals/tasks-focused” (3.3%), “client-low” (18.5%), and “all-low” (8.5%). Longitudinal multilevel models revealed lower current personal functioning after client-low sessions, than after all-high or bond-focused sessions, and higher current psychological symptoms after client-low sessions than after all-high sessions. Clients reported higher next-session symptoms after client-low sessions than after all-high or bond-focused sessions. No difference was detected in outcomes between all-low or goals/tasks-focused sessions and the rest. This study has significant implications for treatment planning, monitoring of the therapeutic alliance, and supervision of therapists-in-training.

articles_hidden.title: Bounded and Unbounded Number Line Estimation in Adults: Accuracy, Response Characteristics, and Mathematical Achievement
articles_hidden.authors: Felix Ayesu; Sharon Henry Yakusi; Valentine Ampah
articles_hidden.abstract:
Number line estimation is widely used to examine numerical magnitude processing and its relationship with mathematics. However,
it remains unclear whether mathematical achievement is more closely associated with estimation accuracy or with characteristics of
estimation responses. The present study examined these relationships among 192 adults who completed bounded and unbounded
number line estimation tasks and mathematics assessments covering arithmetic, fractions, algebra, and percentages. Linear,
logarithmic, mixed log-linear, proportional judgment, and scallop models were compared to characterize estimation responses. We
also evaluated the relationships of estimation accuracy and fitted-response characteristics with mathematical achievement. Linear
models best predicted bounded estimation, whereas mixed log-linear and selected scallop models offered small improvements
for unbounded estimation. Greater linearity and stronger proportional judgment model fit were associated with greater bounded
estimation accuracy, while mixed log-linear characteristics were related to estimation error in both tasks. Bounded estimation accuracy
was more consistently associated with mathematical achievement than unbounded accuracy. Most fitted-response characteristics
accounted for little additional variation in mathematics after considering estimation accuracy, although exploratory analyses indicated
that mixed-model characteristics contributed modest additional information. The findings highlight the value of distinguishing
estimation accuracy from the mathematical characteristics of estimation responses when investigating individual differences in
mathematical achievement.

articles_hidden.title: Harmony on the Plate: Peer Networks and the Maintenance and Adoption of Vegetarianism in Adolescence
articles_hidden.authors: Heike Krüger; Rosaly Severijns; Thomas Grund; Aisling Tiernan; Robert L. Hellpap
articles_hidden.abstract:
Adolescence is a formative period for the development of dietary behaviors, yet little is known about how peer relationships shape vegetarianism during this life stage. Existing research on food-related peer influence has largely relied on cross-sectional or perceptual measures, limiting the ability to disentangle social influence from friendship selection processes. Drawing on theories of social influence and social selection, this study examines the co-evolution of friendship networks and vegetarianism adoption and maintenance among adolescents.
Data stem from the longitudinal SOCIALBOND study conducted in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany, comprising 1,372 students across 22 school cohorts followed from seventh to eighth grade. Using sociometric friendship network data and stochastic actor-oriented models (RSiena), we simultaneously model changes in friendship ties and vegetarianism to disentangle peer influence and friendship selection dynamics.
Peer influence processes emerged more clearly than friendship selection effects. Adolescents in smaller grade-level networks were significantly more likely to maintain vegetarianism when they were connected to more vegetarian peers. No comparable influence effects were observed for the adoption of vegetarianism or within larger grade-level networks. Hence, friendship networks primarily reinforced existing vegetarianism rather than promoting new adoption. Results provide little evidence for friendship selection based on vegetarianism. In smaller year groups, vegetarianism did not significantly shape friendship formation or maintenance. In larger year groups, vegetarian-identifying adolescents were less likely to initiate new friendships, but more likely to maintain existing ties over time.
These findings highlight that adolescent vegetarianism is socially embedded, but that peer dynamics operate mainly through reinforcement mechanisms and vary across network contexts.

articles_hidden.title: The Road to Liberation is Paved with Threats: A Biopsychosocial Perspective on Minoritized Individuals’ Responses to Hierarchy-Disruptive Social Change
articles_hidden.authors: Marty Colombo; Daan Scheepers; Félice van Nunspeet
articles_hidden.abstract: When social equates to social mobility, it elicits adaptive (“challenge”) stress responses among low-status individuals. Instead, hierarchy-disruptive social change may impose under-theorized demands on minoritized individuals, eliciting maladaptive (‘threat’) stress. Thus, LGBTQ+ (n = 57) and cisgender-heterosexual (n = 57) participants expressed their opinion about the status quo and the social change (introducing a non-binary constitution) while cardiovascular challenge-threat was measured. As hypothesized, LGBTQ+ participants exhibited threat when discussing change, compared to the status quo; unexpectedly, cisgender-heterosexual participants exhibited challenge. Among LGBTQ+ participants, higher personal, but not ingroup, demands paired with lower personal resources predicted higher threat. Verbal opinions, coded into five clusters of demands and resources mapped onto challenge-threat, endorsement of change, and protest intentions (but not donations). Notably, one cluster combining failure and retaliation demands with moral hope and collective resources revealed that minoritized individuals persist in social change despite threat, potentially at the cost of their well-being.

articles_hidden.title: Speaking Progress, Feeling Threat: A Biopsychosocial Approach to Systemic Progressive Social Change
articles_hidden.authors: Marty Colombo; Daan Scheepers; Maaike Homan; Félice van Nunspeet
articles_hidden.abstract: Progressive values are substantially endorsed across Western Europe, yet concrete engagement with social change remains limited. This gap raises questions about the motivational and physiological processes that may underlie ambivalence toward progressive action. Drawing on the Biopsychosocial Model of Challenge and Threat (BPS-CT), the present study examined whether progressive hierarchy-disruptive social change elicit cardiovascular threat responses even among individuals who support such change. Ninety Western European university students participated in a within-subjects laboratory study in which they discussed the university’s current collaborations (status quo condition) followed by implementing an academic boycott-like change targeting unethical institutional collaborations (social change condition). Cardiovascular responses were assessed via cardiac output (CO), total peripheral resistance (TPR), and the Threat-Challenge Index (TCI), and analyzed using multilevel modeling. In line with preregistered predictions, the social-change condition elicited stronger physiological threat than the status-quo (lower or stable CO, higher TPR, lower TCI). These responses persisted after controlling for political orientation and (progressive) attitudes, and despite participants generally expressing high support for social change. Text analyses revealed heterogeneity in the sources of threat: Participants either showed reluctance to relinquish status-quo privileges or voiced practical concerns regarding the change. By contrast, relative challenge, which was less prevalent, related to perceiving collective resources to deal with the change but also to rationalization of opposition. These findings suggest that even supporting individuals are not always immune to threat responses when confronting material systemic change.

articles_hidden.title: The Transformative Side of Societal Stress: Threat and Challenge Responses to Progressive Social Changes
articles_hidden.authors: Marty Colombo; Félice van Nunspeet; Daan Scheepers
articles_hidden.abstract: Research showed that social changes elicit threat, which is considered a negative response to be avoided to improve intergroup relations. However, this approach overlooks the transformative potential of positive stress (challenge) for progressive social changes. To address this gap, we investigated whether, and if so, under what conditions, social change is perceived as threatening or challenging. Results from a representative Dutch sample (N = 411) revealed that social change is more threatening than the status quo. Furthermore, the instrumental (vs. symbolic) aspects of change, and its perceived demands and uncertainty heighten threat, while the ingroup and system (vs. personal) dimensions of change, and social resources and support buffer against threat. Our results offer insight into what factors promote more adaptive (challenge) rather than maladaptive (threat) responses to social changes. They encourage a critical perspective on social change, framing threat not as inherently negative but as tensions to be navigated.

articles_hidden.title: What kind of understanding does a behavioural model provide? Warrants for prediction, process and intervention
articles_hidden.authors: Jamal Amani Rad; Stephane Hess; Thomas Hancock
articles_hidden.abstract: Behavioural models are used to forecast outcomes, interpret psychological processes and assess interventions. We develop an account of model warrant centred on the claim being made: a defeasible justification tied to a specified inference, its target conditions and the assumptions connecting a model to behaviour. Predictive, process and intervention warrants identify overlapping evidential obligations rather than a hierarchy or an exhaustive account of understanding. The organising question is whether accounts compatible with the available observations disagree about the conclusion being drawn. An analytical example shows that a binary logit curve can coincide exactly with the choice probabilities of a simple diffusion model, while leaving its temporal commitments untested. We distinguish the additional constraints supplied by response times from the separate requirements of parameter identification, recovery and construct validation. A second constructed example gives two accounts with identical observational choice distributions but different intervention effects. These examples locate the extra assumptions or observations needed to extend a model's interpretation. They also identify conclusions that remain defensible under uncertainty: predictive competence, partial process knowledge and decisions robust across specified alternatives. We propose a concise statement of warrant that connects each substantive claim to its evidence, scope and unresolved alternatives. This approach makes model evaluation more informative for psychological theory without reducing understanding to fit, transparency or an exhaustive description of mechanism.

articles_hidden.title: Same stimuli, different spaces: how task, observer and amount of data influence geometry and reliability of mental representations
articles_hidden.authors: Guillermo Aguilar; Inés Schönmann; Barbara F. Mühlbauer; David-Elias Künstle; Felix Wichmann
articles_hidden.abstract: Similarity is central to explaining categorisation and perception in humans and artificial systems. A popular formulation treats similarity as distance in a multidimensional “mental”, “psychological” or “perceptual” space, in which similar objects lie close together. Modern ordinal embedding algorithms estimate such spaces efficiently from ordinal responses, and even though they are increasingly used to study mental representations, several methodological questions about their application and interpretation remain unresolved. Here, we address these questions with data from extensive, well-controlled psychophysical experiments. We show that popular triplet tasks are potentially more reliable than hitherto believed, but only if the substantial individual differences between observers are not discarded by pooling their responses. Furthermore, pooling across observers also inflates estimates of the dimensionality of the inferred space. To mitigate this, we propose an additional effect size criterion. Finally, we show that two commonly employed triplet tasks presumed to be comparable---classic triplets with a reference and odd-one-out tasks---are psychologically different. Even when stimuli, observers and trial-by-trial presentations are kept constant, they result in different inferred representations, often of lower dimensionality for the odd-one-out task. Spaces derived from the classic task generalise to choices in the odd-one-out task, but not vice versa, suggesting that observers might rely on impoverished decision criteria in the odd-one-out task. Our results demonstrate the potential of triplet tasks and ordinal embedding methods, but also show how seemingly innocuous design choices can impair the reliability and usefulness of the inferred mental representations.

articles_hidden.title: Measuring Intermediate Deep Feature Knowledge in Preparation-for-Learning
articles_hidden.authors: Katharina Ockl; Inga Glogger-Frey
articles_hidden.abstract: In preparation-for-learning, preparation activities can be designed differently and may foster different cognitive processes, resulting in different intermediate knowledge. To understand how preparation-for-learning works and what makes it effective, different kinds of intermediate knowledge must be assessed, but it is challenging and time-consuming to measure intermediate deep-feature knowledge without influencing the learning process itself. We tested two newly developed instruments for measuring intermediate deep-feature knowledge (recognition test, stimulated self-report) in two studies. Correlations between the results from each instrument and a think-aloud measure were used as indicators of convergent validity. Sensitivity was assessed by comparing two preparation activities (high-generative vs. low-generative). In Study 1 (N = 69), neither the stimulated self-report nor the recognition test detected differences between the preparation activities in contrast to the think-aloud measure. The stimulated self-report score was moderately correlated with the think-aloud measure. The recognition test score was not correlated with the think-aloud measure. On the basis of the Study 1 findings, adapted versions of the instruments were tested in Study 2 (N = 39). In line with the results from the think-aloud measure, only the stimulated self-report was more sensitive at detecting better intermediate deep-feature knowledge in the low-generative condition. The self-report score was also significantly correlated with the think-aloud score, whereas the recognition test score was not. Findings suggest that a stimulated self-report with well-designed response options can serve as a nonreactive, sensitive, and valid instrument for measuring intermediate deep-feature knowledge.

articles_hidden.title: When and How Does Post-Encoding Wakeful Rest Benefit Memory? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Wolf Pink; Annika Notbohm; Anna Röschel; Paula Alejandra Porras López; Dilan Barisan; Cornelia Kranczioch; Mandy Roheger
articles_hidden.abstract:
Engaging in short periods of wakeful rest following encoding can benefit later memory retrieval of
encoded material. The magnitude of and mechanisms driving this wakeful rest effect are, however,
unclear. Accordingly, this review's main objectives are 1) estimating an aggregate wakeful rest
effect, 2) identifying the main experimental determinants of the wakeful rest effect, and 3)
synthesizing insights on the mechanisms driving the wakeful rest effect. For this preregistered
meta-analysis (PROSPERO registration number CRD42023487595), we searched Google Scholar,
PubMed, PsycINFO, PsycART, and Web of Science for all peer-reviewed studies of adult healthy
and memory-impaired humans, manipulating participants' post-encoding activities to compare
declarative memory performance between periods of wakeful rest and other activities. Update
searches were conducted on 20.05.2026. The identified studies were assessed for potential risk of
bias using the RoB 2 tool and synthesized in a three-level meta-regression approach. In total, we
included 54 studies with 3673 individual participants contributing data. An aggregate wakeful rest
effect of g = 0.35 (95% CI [0.23, 0.46], p < .001) was found, indicating substantially better memory
performance following post-encoding rest compared to active comparator conditions. Our results
show that the magnitude of the wakeful rest effect depends on several, partially intercorrelated,
experimental characteristics, including population, comparator condition, and memory measure,
and reveal a clear pattern: human declarative memory performance benefits from post-encoding
wakeful rest when demands on our memory system are particularly high.

articles_hidden.title: The Face of Agency: A Reverse Correlation Study
articles_hidden.authors: Sabine Bou Saba; Carl Michael Galang; Marcel Brass
articles_hidden.abstract: As people move through their social environment, they constantly make assumptions about others' abilities and personalities, often relying on personal characteristics as cues. One such characteristic is gender. One robust pattern is that people tend to attribute agency to masculine individuals. Here, we asked whether this relationship holds when approached from the opposite direction: is the representation of agency itself gendered? Using reverse correlation, we conducted two studies to construct a visual representation of agency and examine its associated attributes. In Study 1a, participants completed a traditional reverse correlation task with an androgynous base image, selecting the face that looked more or less agentic depending on their assigned condition. In Study 1b, a separate group of participants rated the resulting classification images (CIs) from Study 1a; agency was represented not as masculine, but as feminine, attractive, and trustworthy. Study 2a replicated Study 1a using a masculine base image instead, and in Study 2b, agency was represented as neither masculine nor feminine, but again as trustworthy and attractive. Together, these studies suggest that agency is not represented in a gendered way, but rather through attractiveness and trustworthiness, indicating that agency may be best captured by socially desirable traits more broadly, rather than by gender.

articles_hidden.title: Does facial expression processing require attention? A multi-lab replication of Eimer et al. (2003)
articles_hidden.authors: Ziyi Wang; Alejandro Estudillo; Ala Yankouskaya; Nazanin S. Andalibi; Amy Bland; Chris Robert Harrison Brown; Elisabeth Fonteneau; Donovan G. Govan; Marine Granjon; Tijl Grootswagers
articles_hidden.abstract: How the brain processes facial expressions and whether this process requires focal attention have been central topics of neurophysiological research on face processing. In a seminal study, using scalp-recorded event-related potentials (ERPs), Eimer, Holmes, and McGlone (2003) found that emotional and neutral faces were differently processed in the brain as early as 160 ms after stimulus onset. Importantly, these ERP differences disappeared when attention was directed away from the face stimuli, suggesting the necessity of focal attention in facial expression processing. These results have greatly motivated further research in the field. Yet, subsequent research did not always agree with these findings, and the study was never directly replicated. Hence, this study has been selected by #EEGManyLabs, a global and multi-laboratory replication project, for a high-powered direct replication across multiple laboratories (N = 41 in each laboratory). We hypothesize the replication of the original positive findings, including the ERP effects differentiating emotional and neutral faces and their dependence on focal attention. To address the debate on facial expression processing and the role of N170, we will also take this opportunity to reassess key negative findings of the original study, namely no difference between emotional and neutral facial expressions in N170 and no ERP differences among the six facial expressions. Replication or revision of these findings will confirm the necessity of focal attention in emotional face processing and the postulated biomarkers of basic emotion processing. This study will provide a reproducible benchmark on face processing.

articles_hidden.title: Working With Circular Data: A Tutorial for Cognitive and Behavioral Research
articles_hidden.authors: Stella Wernicke; Julie de Falco; Zahara Gironés; Chris Jungerius; Ivan Tomic; Adam Triabhall; Xiaolu Wang; Paul Bays
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introductory statistics courses and conventional methods in behavioral and cognitive science are typically restricted to Euclidean space without explicitly stating this, leaving many researchers unaware of how to handle data with circular or periodic properties (e.g., time of day or orientation on a screen). This tutorial provides an accessible yet rigorous introduction, designed to bridge the gap between statistical theory and practical application. After an overview of common applications, we discuss different ways of representing circular data mathematically and fundamental principles for working with them. We explain angular and vector representations and operations, including key considerations for implementing them in computer code. We then survey methods for visualizing circular data, including linear and polar plots and presentation of summary statistics. Next, we discuss circular measures of central tendency, dispersion, and shape: how they relate to their Euclidean counterparts and why they differ. Finally, we turn to more advanced topics of the kind needed to construct models of circular data. We introduce the most common circular distribution families, including circular analogs of the Gaussian distribution and their properties, as well as flexible distribution families that can describe skewed and heavy-tailed data. The tutorial takes a method-oriented approach, not tied to specific software, but highlighting factors relevant to experimental design, data analysis, and statistical modeling. A consistent theme is the need to rigorously account for the inherent periodicity of circular data. We also provide a consistent notation for circular statistics and parameters, addressing the lack of established conventions in the field.
