articles_hidden.title: Questionable mediated effect of physical activity on smartphone addiction: A comment on Fu and Wang (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen
articles_hidden.abstract: Drawing on the covariance matrix reported by Fu and Wang, I reassessed the empirical basis of their mediation model linking physical activity to decreased smartphone addiction. I demonstrate that the observed covariance structure can be reproduced by a theoretically different latent-variable model that does not rely on the directional mechanism proposed in the original article. In this alternative account, self-reported physical activity, self-control, health-promoting lifestyle, and smartphone addiction are conceptualized as indicators of a broader construct, core self-evaluation. The results illustrate a broader inferential problem in psychological research: multiple theoretically plausible models may provide equally adequate explanations of the same correlational pattern. Consequently, observational associations alone offer limited grounds for preferring one explanation over competing alternatives. Researchers should therefore routinely evaluate alternative models when drawing inferences about psychological mechanisms from nonexperimental data.

articles_hidden.title: Statistical theory of strategic delay under a deadline
articles_hidden.authors: Mattia Eluchans; Gian Luca Lancia; Rava Azeredo da Silveira; Giovanni Pezzulo
articles_hidden.abstract: Delaying the start of tasks with deadlines is a widespread phenomenon that occurs across multiple domains. While delaying tasks can be maladaptive, here we propose that, in some situations, it results from an optimal time-management strategy. We propose a theoretical model of the strategic delay of the initiation of tasks with deadlines that relies on an unavoidable aspect of any projection into the future, namely, that the time it takes to complete a task is variable. This fundamental assumption distinguishes our theory from alternative theoretical accounts that invoke specific structures of preferences or costs to elucidate the occurrence of (adaptive or maladaptive) task-initiation delays. Our model captures the basic features of strategic delay and predicts a phenomenon that we demonstrate empirically, the ‘farther-earlier’ effect: decision-makers who live farther to their destinations (e.g., schools or offices) tend to arrive earlier than those who live closer. The same theory explains the widely documented tendency to repeatedly delay the initiation of a task (e.g., drafting a grant application) as the deadline for the completion of the task approaches. Our framework thus puts forth a normative theory in which various manifestations of strategic delay reflect an optimal adaptation to environmental statistics.

articles_hidden.title: Music mood regulation across adulthood: Age-related changes in strategies and their underlying functions
articles_hidden.authors: Catherine Tan; Alessandro Ansani; Laura Cirelli; Suvi Saarikallio
articles_hidden.abstract: Aging is related to changes in the usage of emotion regulation strategies due to shifting motivational goals, life experience, and declines in physiological, cognitive, and social resources. Music supports the facilitation of music mood regulation strategies (i.e., Entertainment, Revival, Strong Sensation, Diversion, Discharge, Mental Work, and Solace), but age-related changes in their usage and underlying psychological functions remain underexplored across adulthood. The current cross-sectional study addresses this gap by having 250 participants (M age = 40.88 years, SD age = 17.78, range = 18 - 87) complete the Brief Music in Mood Regulation Scale (Saarikallio, 2012) and experimenter-created items exploring how much the aforementioned strategies are facilitated through serving Bodily, Cognitive, or Social functions. Regression models showed that older participants use less music for mood regulation. This trend was observed in all strategies except Revival, whose use remained stable over time. Linear Mixed-Effect models showed that music resonated in participants’ bodies to facilitate Entertainment and Revival, while it helped with cognitive thought and emotion processing for Mental Work. The remaining strategies were underpinned by both Bodily and Cognitive functions. No age differences were observed here. These results contribute to the understanding of music-based mood regulation and promote music as a psychoeducational, health, and wellbeing tool for all ages.

articles_hidden.title: Impossibility and Logical Contradictions Can Enhance the Perceived Value of Fictional Theological Propositions
articles_hidden.authors: Takuetsu Yajima; Eisuke Niida; Yo Nakawake
articles_hidden.abstract: Supernatural concepts are often thought to gain cultural attraction by violating intuitive expectations in limited ways, but many theological doctrines also involve logical contradictions or impossibilities. It remains unclear how such formal violations influence people’s evaluations of religious propositions. In the present study, 96 Japanese adults rated 20 fictional theological propositions on dimensions related to perceived value, including importance, profundity, interestingness, sacredness, and shareability. Those propositions were rated for impossibility and logical contradiction. A composite positive-evaluation score was derived from items rating perceived value and analyzed using linear mixed-effects models. The result shows higher impossibility and higher logical contradiction predict higher positive evaluations of the propositions. These findings suggest that impossible and contradictory theological content can be positively evaluated.

articles_hidden.title: Optimizing threat expectancy change during exposure therapy for anxiety disorders: Study protocol for a mechanism-focused two-arm parallel group randomized controlled superiority trial with sequential Bayes factor design
articles_hidden.authors: Andre Pittig; Lena Waltemate; Simon Edward Blackwell; Roxana Pittig
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Anxiety disorders are highly prevalent and associated with significant personal and 
societal burden. Exposure-based cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is a first-line treatment, yet 
response varies widely, with remission rates of 50–70% and relapse in 5–14% of patients. Targeting 
mechanisms of change underlying successful exposure-based CBT may improve treatment efficacy. 
This study aims to optimize exposure-based CBT by enhancing learning rates through tailored post-
exposure processing focused on threat expectancy change. 
Methods: This is a two-arm parallel-group randomized controlled superiority trial comparing 
optimized exposure with post-exposure processing versus exposure without post-processing in adults 
with panic disorder, agoraphobia, social anxiety disorder, or specific phobia. The primary outcome is 
the exposure-related learning rate, calculated from patients’ threat expectancy ratings before and 
after exposure. A predefined sequential Bayes factor design is used to evaluate evidence 
continuously, with a maximum sample size of 70 per group. Secondary outcomes include threat 
expectancy change, cognitive immunization processes, and longitudinal trajectories of expectancy 
change assessed via ecological momentary assessment (EMA). Data are collected within manualized 
exposure-based CBT, including standardized exposure worksheets, psychometric assessments, and 
EMA. 
Discussion: This study represents a novel, mechanism-focused approach to optimizing exposure-
based CBT. By prioritizing the enhancement of learning rates over symptom reduction in the first 
step, the trial increases feasibility, efficiency, and scientific rigor. If successful, this approach could 
inform personalized, adaptive treatment protocols that target core mechanisms of change. The 
findings may advance process-based psychotherapy and improve long-term outcomes for anxiety 
disorders.

articles_hidden.title: Direct and indirect mental interaction on random binary event generators:  an updated meta-analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Patrizio Tressoldi; Michael Duggan
articles_hidden.abstract:
This updated meta-analysis evaluated evidence for direct and indirect mental interactions with random binary event generators (RNGs) in studies published after the meta-analysis by Bösch, Steinkamp, and Boller (2006). The aim was to estimate the overall magnitude and precision of reported effects, assess between-study heterogeneity and potential publication bias, and compare findings across direct intention and indirect field-based protocols.
	Studies were identified through database searches, specialist journals and conference proceedings, an AI-assisted literature search, and contact with researchers in the field. Forty-nine eligible studies were included: 18 direct-interaction studies, in which participants intentionally attempted to influence RNG outputs, and 28 indirect-interaction studies, in which RNG activity was examined in relation to collective human attention.
Direct interaction studies showed a small positive overall per trial effect size d = 0.0017, 95% CI [0.0001, 0.0033], p = .041; I² = 0%. Indirect interaction studies showed a larger but statistically non-significant and less precise effect size estimate, d = 0.0006, 95% CI [-0.00001-0.0012], p = .064; I² = 25.2%).
	Moderator analyses of direct studies suggested larger effects among selected participants and in bidirectional-intention tasks, although these estimates were imprecise and based on few studies. 	Selection-model, excess-significance, and proportion-of-significant-results analyses indicated possible publication bias in both research paradigms.
	Overall, the findings suggest small deviations from chance in direct RNG-interaction studies, whereas evidence for indirect effects remains uncertain because of lower precision. Potential selective reporting and the limited number of studies constrain firm conclusions, highlighting the need for preregistered, adequately powered, and independently replicated investigations.

articles_hidden.title: Mapping Adolescents’ Experiences with Depression and Psychotherapy Using A Mixed-Methods Approach to Tailor Youth Assessment
articles_hidden.authors: Jennifer Xiu-Rong Chen; Bennett Kleinberg; Melissa Miléna De Smet
articles_hidden.abstract:
Abstract
Depression is a debilitating condition that is highly prevalent among adolescents. However, depression is often understood through a nomothetic lens, meaning that there is a tendency to measure general patterns of symptoms. This risks overgeneralisation that largely ignores the individual, lived experiences of depressed youth. We develop and demonstrate a mixed-methods assessment approach in which participants can identify and elaborate on what lived experiences are important to them in therapy. Participants were 21 university students (M = 20.5, SD = 1.3) who had attended some form of psychotherapy in the past 2 years. Participants first performed a statement-sorting task, in which they rate the subjective importance of youth-identified experiences of depression and psychotherapy. This task is followed by an interview on their reasons for prioritising statements. Descriptives of the statement ratings indicated that there was a high variability in how the statements were rated. Thematic analysis was conducted to examine this heterogeneity, and to explain why participants had different priorities. The generated themes concerned: 1) different rationales for prioritisation of problems when navigating core problems versus “minor” problems, 2) differences in the effect of trust in the therapist on the course of therapy, 3) the degree to which one’s mental health concerns are part of one’s identity, and 4) if and how individuals chose to accept social support. These findings underscore the variety in psychotherapy experiences, and suggest the need to prioritise different things in psychotherapy assessment through a tailored approach.

articles_hidden.title: BEYOND BINARY COUNTS: SEVERITY-WEIGHTED ADVERSE CHILDHOOD EXPERIENCES IMPROVE PREDICTION OF PSYCHOSOCIAL OUTCOMES IN PREGNANT WOMEN
articles_hidden.authors: Marta Giménez-Dasí; Sandra Doval; Joel Angulo-Rodríguez; María Cea-Vicente; Mónica Díaz de Neira Hernando; Marta Fernández Sánchez; Fatima Garcia Benasach; Aitana Gomis Pomares; Miguel Ángel Marín Gabriel; Gema Martin Seoane
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are typically operationalized as binary indicators (present/absent), collapsing heterogeneous exposure levels into a single count. Whether preserving severity gradations improves the prediction of adult health outcomes remains an open empirical question with direct
implications for research and clinical screening.
Objective: To systematically compare binary versus severity-weighted ACE operationalizations across multiple levels of data representation (item-level, domain-level, and sum scores), analytic frameworks (sum scores, exploratory factor analysis, item response theory, and penalized regression), and psychosocial
outcomes in a perinatal cohort.
Method: Participants were 454 pregnant women recruited within a longitudinal project on early experiences and perinatal mental health. ACEs were assessed using an expanded ACE/ACE-IQ-based instrument capturing both occurrence and severity of 30 adversity items across 17 domains. Five outcomes were measured: depressive symptoms, prenatal psychosocial adjustment, resilience, social support, and benevolent childhood experiences. Ten distinct ACE data representations were constructed. Predictive validity was evaluated using repeated 10-fold cross-validation with honest estimation (factor models refit inside each training fold).
Results: Severity-weighted operationalizations consistently outperformed binary counterparts across all comparisons. The largest advantage emerged when the severity-graded domain scores were retained as separated predictors. Factor-based representations showed comparable predictive performance but poor structural adequacy and computational instability. The severity advantage was consistent at every level of comparison.
Conclusions: Preserving severity information in ACE measurement was associated with greater out-ofsample predictive performance than binary scoring in this perinatal cohort. These findings support considering severity-weighted, domain-specific scoring in future ACE research and warrant further evaluation of its potential utility in clinical screening.
Keywords: Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs); severity-weighted scoring; perinatal mental health; predictive validity; cross-validation;

articles_hidden.title: A Tutorial on Safe Anytime-Valid Inference: Practical Maximally Flexible Sampling Designs for Experiments Based on e-Values
articles_hidden.authors: Alexander Ly; Udo Boehm; Peter Grünwald; Aaditya Ramdas; Don van Ravenzwaaij
articles_hidden.abstract: We demonstrate how e-values simplify both experimental design and the inference process. With e-values researchers can perform anytime-valid tests and construct confidence intervals that maintain type I error control regardless of the sample size. This enables real-time monitoring of evidence as data are collected, permitting early termination of experiments without intolerably inflating the risk of false discoveries. Early stopping not only con- serves resources, but also mitigates risk for participants in clinical settings. Anytime-valid tests allow for optional continuation, that is, the extension of an experiment, for instance if more funds become available, or even if the evidence looks promising and the funding agency, a reviewer, or an editor urges the experimenter to collect more data. Analogously, a researcher can be assured that a 95% anytime-valid confidence interval will, with at least 95% probability, cover the true effect size regardless of how, or even if, data collection is stopped. We use the free and open-source software package safestats implemented in R to illustrate the practical benefits of this novel inference framework.

articles_hidden.title: Transparency Is Necessary but Not Sufficient for Trust: Information Leakage and Procedural Overfitting in Supervised Machine Learning for Psychology
articles_hidden.authors: Rosa Lavelle-Hill
articles_hidden.abstract: Min et al. (2026) provide a timely checklist for improving the transparency and trust of supervised machine learning (ML) research in psychology. I strongly endorse this goal and recognize that their focus on retrospective reporting is both valuable and the appropriate scope for an article. However, I suggest that two related issues warrant greater emphasis in their framework: information leakage and procedural overfitting. Both can produce optimistic estimates of model performance despite apparently transparent reporting. I propose two extensions to the checklist: reporting requirements that make information leakage auditable and prospective specification of key analytical decisions through preregistration. I argue that these additions would further strengthen the ability of readers and reviewers to evaluate the trustworthiness of supervised ML analyses in psychology. Moreover, comprehensive guidelines that do not sufficiently emphasize these issues may create unwarranted confidence that threats to valid model evaluation have been ruled out, allowing information leakage or procedural overfitting to remain undetected.

articles_hidden.title: Effects of perturbation magnitude and duration on sense of agency and electrodermal activity during continuous action
articles_hidden.authors: Yuanhao Lin; Mizuki Kira; Maiko Kobayashi; Katsumi Watanabe; Kanji Tanaka
articles_hidden.abstract: Sense of agency (SoA) refers to the subjective feeling of controlling one’s own actions and their outcomes. Previous studies have shown that sensorimotor discrepancies, such as spatial perturbations, reduce SoA, but it remains unclear whether such control disruptions also elicit online autonomic arousal during continuous action. In the present study, across two experiments, participants performed a continuous target-reaching task in which visual feedback of cursor movement was spatially perturbed. We recorded electrodermal activity during the task and used skin conductance level (SCL) as the physiological measure. We assessed subjective SoA and perceived stress after each trial. In Experiment 1, we manipulated perturbation magnitude and found that stronger perturbation reduced subjective SoA, increased perceived stress, and elicited a greater increase in SCL. In Experiment 2, we manipulated perturbation duration to examine whether the SCL increase in Experiment 1 depended on the continued presence of a strong perturbation or primarily on the early phase of disrupted control. Participants reported lower subjective SoA and higher perceived stress in the Long-term perturbation condition than in the Short-term perturbation condition, whereas mean SCL change did not reliably differ between conditions. Together, these findings suggest that spatial perturbations during continuous action are accompanied by changes in sympathetic electrodermal activity. The SCL was sensitive to perturbation magnitude, whereas evidence for a duration-related difference in mean SCL was limited.

articles_hidden.title: Perceived Neighborhood Disorder, Social Vulnerability,  and Intimate Partner Violence  Among Adults over 60
articles_hidden.authors: Judith Biesen; Joeci Orth
articles_hidden.abstract: Objective: Although neighborhood disadvantage has been linked to intimate partner violence (IPV) in younger and middle-aged adults, its role in late-life IPV is understudied. This study examined whether perceived neighborhood disorder (PND) and zip code-level social vulnerability (i.e., subjective and objective attributes of neighborhood disadvantage) are associated with psychological and physical IPV perpetration and victimization in adults 60 and older. Method: Participants in committed relationships (N = 380) completed an online survey assessing past-year aggression, PND, loneliness, and the zip code of their primary residence. Zip codes were linked to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s Social Vulnerability Index (SVI). Hierarchical logistic regression models estimated associations of PND and overall SVI with each IPV outcome. Exploratory analyses replaced the overall SVI with its four themes and the total PND with its four subscales. Results: Greater PND was associated with increased odds of physical, but not psychological, IPV perpetration and victimization. Greater social vulnerability was associated with greater odds of psychological aggression perpetration and victimization, as well as physical aggression victimization. These associations remained significant after false discovery rate correction. Conclusions: Both subjective and objective aspects of neighborhood disadvantage are linked to IPV in older adults’ committed relationships, even after controlling for sociodemographic characteristics and loneliness as an individual risk factor. These results suggest the need for geographically targeted allocation of IPV resources to socially vulnerable neighborhoods, as well as for late-life IPV screening research that considers the neighborhood environment.

articles_hidden.title: Bringing Interoception Into the Clinical Setting of Alcohol Use Disorder
articles_hidden.authors: Fiorella Macchiavello; Juan Pablo Morales; Mario Villena-Gonzalez; Germán Campos-Arteaga; Martín Laferte; Felipe Rojas Thomas
articles_hidden.abstract:
Abstract
Background. Interoception is increasingly implicated in alcohol use disorder (AUD), yet clinical translation
remains limited by construct conflation, dependence on cardiac tasks, and uncertainty about whether atypical
bodily processing reflects a stable deficit or a context-sensitive process.
Methods. This critical narrative review integrates AUD-specific behavioral, psychophysiological,
neuroimaging, alcohol-administration, and intervention evidence using an explicit hierarchy that separates
direct interoceptive measures from mechanistic and translational support.
Results. Direct studies indicate that lower cardiac-task performance can coexist with heightened subjective
bodily attention, while recent validity work shows that heartbeat-counting scores cannot be treated as pure
indices of bodily-signal detection. Acute alcohol, stress-cue, and ambulatory findings further indicate that the
behavioral significance of bodily signals depends on how they are generated, attributed, and linked to
alcohol-related action.
Conclusions. The central clinical proposition is not to increase bodily awareness indiscriminately, but to
improve the detection, differentiation, attribution, and appraisal of bodily states within context. This
signal-context-action framework generates testable hypotheses for assessment, relapse monitoring, and
treatment matching within established AUD care

articles_hidden.title: Stereotype fragments positive impressions of disadvantaged groups
articles_hidden.authors: Yuqing Shi; Daniel DongWon Oh
articles_hidden.abstract: The halo effect reflects a fundamental bias in person perception: humans infer multiple positive qualities from a single trait, assuming traits cohere. Here we show that this coherence depends on targets’ social status and perceivers’ stereotype endorsement. Across four correlational datasets and two experiments examining gender, age, economic status, mental health, and novel groups (total N = 623), perceivers high in stereotype endorsement showed weaker coherence between warmth and competence inferences for disadvantaged than for advantaged targets. In preregistered experiments with novel groups, learning a low-competence stereotype weakened conceptual trait coherence, and after learning only about group status, the coherence gap scaled with the competence stereotypes participants formed. These findings reveal a subtle form of bias: stereotypes fragment the cognitive scaffolding of impression formation, imposing unequal burdens on members of marginalized groups.

articles_hidden.title: Is Fixed Mindset Theory… Fixed?
articles_hidden.authors: Ash Buchanan
articles_hidden.abstract: Search for the definition of a fixed mindset today and you’ll likely encounter a single theory presented as settled fact: Carol Dweck’s definition. You might even hear that Dweck coined the phrase in 2006. Yet a broader history tells a different story. The earliest identified description comes from intelligence analyst Richards Heuer in 1981, while the idea has roots that stretch back even further. This invites an interesting inquiry: for a field that talks so much about growth, how much of a learn-it-all attitude have we brought to our understanding of fixed mindset? Perhaps one of the most interesting tests of a growth mindset is what we do when we discover that the story we thought we knew is not the whole story. This perspectives paper explores this broader history of fixed mindset and asks: Who gets to decide what a fixed mindset is? Has an entire generation of people inherited a fixed idea of what fixed mindset means? And what might become possible if we learn from a broader range of perspectives, including our own lived experiences?

articles_hidden.title: Neurospirituality Reappraised: Brain Mechanisms of Transcendent Experience and Beyond
articles_hidden.authors: Marleide da Mota Gomes
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background:
Subjective experiences featuring altered self-awareness, temporal perception, or spatial boundaries—termed Non-Ordinary Experiences (NOEs)—occur across clinical neurology, psychiatry, and psychedelic medicine, including in insular ecstatic seizures, meditation, breathwork, hypnosis, and psychedelic therapy. 
Objective:
To synthesize neurobiological and clinical literature on NOEs for neurologists by presenting three heuristic frameworks: 
1.	A six-dimension phenomenological taxonomy; 
2.	A tri-level descriptive taxonomy (computational "software", neuromodulatory-autonomic "firmware", and network "hardware"); 
3.	The Trigger–Dynamic Psyche–4E Appraisal–Outcome Model, which maps how acute neurodynamic shifts resolve into adaptive growth or clinical distress without reducing existential meaning to neural activity. 
Methods:
Narrative synthesis of systematic reviews, coordinate-based meta-analyses, and key theoretical frameworks sourced via PubMed/MEDLINE. 
Results:
Conflating spirituality, religion, and NOEs causes construct contamination in neuroimaging, compounded by unvalidated single-item measures and non-independent cohorts. An fMRI meta-analysis of meditation (34 studies, N=700) reveals aggregate recruitment of the right rolandic operculum, left insula, supplementary motor area, and hippocampus, arguing against a singular "spiritual center". First-person reports are mapped using a six-dimension schema (experiential content, temporal dynamics, spatial dynamics, volitional dynamics/agency, ownership/embodiment, cognitive stance). Mechanistically, states are organized across three bidirectionally coupled levels: computational inference ("software"), neuromodulatory-autonomic state-setting ("firmware"), and large-scale networks ("hardware"). Five entry routes (meditation, psychedelics, breathwork, hypnosis, focal neurological events) are hypothesized to share shifts in Bayesian precision weighting and network decoupling within the master Trigger–Dynamic Psyche–4E Appraisal–Outcome Model. Crucially, long-term outcomes (integration vs. distress) are not dictated by acute brain states alone, but are mediated by contextual filtering through the 4E Appraisal Prism (embodied, embedded, enacted, extended dimensions). 
Conclusions:
Neurospirituality bridges network neuroscience, clinical neurology, and person-centered care. Clarifying biological substrates does not resolve existential validity. Clinicians must maintain a strict distinction between biological mechanisms, subjective experiences, and personal meanings (the Epistemological Invariant) to avoid pathologizing adaptive states or romanticizing neurological disease. 
Key terms: Spirituality; Neuroimaging; Meditation; Hallucinogens; Epilepsy.

articles_hidden.title: Optimizing Open-Ended Interview Assessment Using Response-Based Semantic Indices
articles_hidden.authors: Zihan Yan; Ashley Sylvara; Ziang Xiao; Susu Zhang; Tianjun Sun
articles_hidden.abstract: Open-ended interviews provide rich, behaviorally grounded data for psychological assessment but are often lengthy, redundant, and difficult to optimize due to the lack of quantitative item-level metrics. The present study proposes a response-based semantic framework to optimize open-ended interviews using two indices: semantic discrimination (SD), which captures the extent to which responses align with the target construct, and information coverage (IC), which reflects semantic overlap between responses to a question and responses to other questions, with lower values indicating less redundant information. These indices are combined within a utility-based selection procedure that prioritizes construct-relevant questions while varying the degree of semantic overlap across selected questions. We demonstrate this framework using archival data from a 34-question chatbot-based personality interview. We generated optimized question sequences and evaluated shortened forms in terms of convergent validity with Big Five self-reports, discriminant structure, and measurement efficiency. Results indicate that interview length can often be reduced substantially while retaining convergent validity, with many conditions reaching 80% of peak validity within roughly one-third of the full interview. This approach extends psychometric principles to open-ended assessment by leveraging response content directly, offering a potential scalable method for interview optimization, refinement, and adaptive administration.

articles_hidden.title: JOL Reactivity in Deese-Roediger-McDermott Lists
articles_hidden.authors: No authors listed
articles_hidden.abstract: Making judgments of learning (JOLs) during study often affects later test performance, a phenomenon called JOL reactivity (Double et al., 2018; Ingendahl et al., 2025). JOL reactivity has been observed across several word memory tasks. Some researchers have supposed that JOLs induce item-specific processing (Senkova & Otani, 2021), and others have supposed that JOLs induced relational processing (Chang & Brainerd, 2024). However, research on how JOLs impact false memory remains relatively limited. The goal of the present study was to characterize JOL reactivity in the Deese-Roediger-McDermott (DRM) false memory paradigm. In each experiment, participants studied intermixed DRM lists in either a JOL condition, a passive study condition, or a dual-task control condition. In the first experiment, JOLs enhanced correct recall relative to dual-task controls. However, JOLs had no significant impact on false recall in either experiment. Results were inconsistent with hypotheses that suppose JOLs encourage item-specific or relational processing.
